skills.description: Use when you have SimAb run outputs (run_sum(n).txt files with [(x/H) of the planet]/[(X/H) of the sun]) and need to classify subsolar vs supersolar metallicity and compute C/O ratios to trace the source of heavy elements.
skills.name: co-ratio-abundance-analysis
skills.search_text: co-ratio-abundance-analysis Use when you have SimAb run outputs (run_sum(n).txt files with [(x/H) of the planet]/[(X/H) of the sun]) and need to classify subsolar vs supersolar metallicity and compute C/O ratios to trace the source of heavy elements. When only a single simulation with fully user-specified initial conditions is needed — use the Srun.py single-run mode instead of a multi-run composition analysis. When the question is whether the initial core mass matters — the paper shows the initial protoplanet core mass does not influence the final atmospheric composition, so core mass is not a useful discriminator here. When inputs are raw observables (e.g., spectra) rather than SimAb composition outputs — this skill operates on SimAb's (x/H) ratio files, not on atmospheric retrieval data. This is the paper's core diagnostic for constraining where and from what material giant planets formed. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202141455

skills.description: Use when reconstructing HyLight Case B hydrogen level-population solvers or line emissivities for photoionised nebular gas where collisional excitation from the ground state must enter the rate-equation system (ne up to ~1e2 cm**(-3), T ~1e4 K).
skills.name: collisional-excitation-rate-inclusion
skills.search_text: collisional-excitation-rate-inclusion Use when reconstructing HyLight Case B hydrogen level-population solvers or line emissivities for photoionised nebular gas where collisional excitation from the ground state must enter the rate-equation system (ne up to ~1e2 cm**(-3), T ~1e4 K). When modelling gas conditions far outside typical photoionised nebular conditions (e.g. very high densities where the Case B assumption or the 1-per-cent Cloudy agreement no longer holds) When a Case A solution is required — the reference workflow uses caseB=True; switching the case changes the physical model When only recombination cascades matter and the question explicitly excludes collisional processes; setting coll=False would then be the intended configuration rather than this skill Enables collisional-excitation terms (coll=True) when solving hydrogen level populations in HyLight's HIAtom, so that the steady-state rate equations include collisional excitation from the ground state alongside radiative recombination cascades. This is essential for reproducing reference outputs such as the 3p population of 1.64e-17 cm**(-3) and H alpha emissivity of 3.451e-21 erg/(cm**3*s) at ne=100 cm**(-3), T=1e4 K. astronomy/v1 10.1093/mnras/stag429

This is essential for reproducing reference outputs such as the 3p population of 1.64e-17 cm**(-3) and H alpha emissivity of 3.451e-21 erg/(cm**3*s) at ne=100 cm**(-3), T=1e4 K.

skills.description: Use when you need to reproduce a 1D collisionless-shock discretisation study with Vlasiator, e.g. to check whether a hybrid-Vlasov model departs from fluid (MHD) theory at coarse resolutions like ~1000 km.
skills.name: collisionless-shock-initialization
skills.search_text: collisionless-shock-initialization Use when you need to reproduce a 1D collisionless-shock discretisation study with Vlasiator, e.g. to check whether a hybrid-Vlasov model departs from fluid (MHD) theory at coarse resolutions like ~1000 km. Input plasma is well described by single-fluid MHD and you only need the cheaper MHD-like answer; the point of this skill is to resolve departures from fluid theory, not to replicate MHD. The system of interest requires full global magnetospheric geometry (2D/3D magnetosphere coupling) rather than the 1D shock benchmark; this skill covers only the 1D normal-incidence-style shock setup. You need self-consistent electron kinetics — in Vlasiator electrons are treated as an MHD fluid, so purely electron-scale kinetic questions are out of scope. http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 http://edamontology.org/topic_3855 Configure and run a 1D collisionless shock benchmark in the Vlasiator hybrid-Vlasov solver under terrestrial bow-shock-like plasma conditions, at two grid resolutions (1000 km and 200 km), to test whether kinetic (non-fluid) shock physics is captured and quantify how refinement improves physical detail. astronomy/v1 10.1007/s41115-018-0003-2
skills.summary: Configure and run a 1D collisionless shock benchmark in the Vlasiator hybrid-Vlasov solver under terrestrial bow-shock-like plasma conditions, at two grid resolutions (1000 km and 200 km), to test whether kinetic (non-fluid) shock physics is captured and quantify how refinement improves physical detail.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input plasma is well described by single-fluid MHD and you only need the cheaper MHD-like answer; the point of this skill is to resolve departures from fluid theory, not to replicate MHD. The system of interest requires full global magnetospheric geometry (2D/3D magnetosphere coupling) rather than the 1D shock benchmark; this skill covers only the 1D normal-incidence-style shock setup. You need self-consistent electron kinetics — in Vlasiator electrons are treated as an MHD fluid, so purely electron-scale kinetic questions are out of scope.

The geometry is a spherical distribution with a central point source or an isotropic background on a sphere rather than the semi-infinite slab in an isotropic background — the benchmark ratios (1.8, 11, 6.3, 3.2) are specific to the Slab2Bgnd configuration. skills.search_text: compas-output-data-handling Use when the task requires extracting progenitor binary properties (e.g. ZAMS total mass m1+m2) from COMPAS population-synthesis output files by filtering systems that merge within a Hubble time and match the 90% credible intervals of a specific GW event. The task needs accurate cosmic merger rates: the paper notes an accurate calculation requires convolution of metallicity-specific redshift-dependent star formation rate with the time-delay distribution, which was not done in this dataset. The analysis targets non-BBH outcomes (e.g. Galactic neutron stars, X-ray binaries) or non-Fiducial COMPAS model variations; this skill is built around the fiducial-model BBH output at Z=0.002 and Z=0.001. The event of interest is not GW150914, GW151226 or LVT151012, since the validation thresholds are specific to those three events' posteriors. Loads fiducial COMPAS double compact object population output at Z=0.002 and Z=0.001 from the COMPAS Zenodo community deposit, filters merging binary black holes, and tabulates zero-age-main-sequence progenitor total masses matched to observed gravitational-wave events. It exists to reproduce the paper's progenitor initial-mass ranges for GW150914, GW151226 and LVT151012. astronomy/v1 10.1038/ncomms14906

skills.search_text: compressible-euler-equation-discretization Use when a stationary 2-D gas flow in a galactic potential with a rotating weak bar must be computed by discretizing the compressible isothermal Euler equations, or when reproducing the galax2d solver behavior. The flow is non-isothermal or requires an energy equation / shock heating — galax2d closes the system with p = c_s^2 * rho only. The goal is a fully time-dependent evolution rather than a stationary solution forced by a rotating weak bar. The bar is strong or the domain is 3-D — outside the 2-D weak-bar regime the paper parameterizes. Method for discretizing the 2-D compressible isothermal Euler equations (closed by p = c_s^2 * rho) with axisymmetric galactic-potential and rotating-weak-bar source terms on a Cartesian finite-volume grid, as implemented in the galax2d Matlab package (Mulder 2015), to obtain a stationary barred-galaxy gas flow. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2015.03.005

skills.search_text: concurrent-request-latency-measurement Use when estimating server capacity for tile-based image streaming: you need to measure requests-per-second and latency as concurrent 256×256 tile requests scale up on a multi-core server. Input data is not full-precision (32-bit floating point) scientific imagery served as 256×256 tiles — capacity numbers will not transfer. The goal is client-side or network bandwidth measurement rather than server-side tile serving capacity. The server architecture is distributed or multi-server; this benchmark characterizes a single 12-core server only. Benchmark how tile serving rate and per-request latency scale with concurrency on a single web server, using a modified Apache Bench client against a FastCGI tile server, to quantify how many concurrent users a server comfortably handles for full 32-bit astronomy imagery. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2014.12.006

skills.description: Use when raw ECCOplanets equilibrium condensation output (element/molecule abundances vs temperature, 2000-300 K) shows numerical glitches or jagged curves that must be cleaned before extracting 50% condensation temperatures or ∆Tc trends.

skills.search_text: condensation-curve-smoothing Use when raw ECCOplanets equilibrium condensation output (element/molecule abundances vs temperature, 2000-300 K) shows numerical glitches or jagged curves that must be cleaned before extracting 50% condensation temperatures or ∆Tc trends. You need to change the scientific assumptions of the condensation calculation itself (gas-minimisation setup, molecule set, pressure) — that belongs in simulation.py, not post-processing You want to expand the thermochemical or stellar abundance databases (s4adding_data.py) rather than clean an existing simulation result The raw abundance curves are already smooth and the 50% condensation temperatures reproduce benchmark values — unnecessary cleaning could distort the curves http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 http://edamontology.org/topic_3855 Post-processing of ECCOplanets Gibbs-free-energy-minimisation condensation simulations to clean raw abundance-vs-temperature curves: cropping the gas phase, recomputing glitched sections, removing numerical glitches, and smoothing before extracting condensation temperatures. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202244850
skills.summary: Post-processing of ECCOplanets Gibbs-free-energy-minimisation condensation simulations to clean raw abundance-vs-temperature curves: cropping the gas phase, recomputing glitched sections, removing numerical glitches, and smoothing before extracting condensation temperatures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to change the scientific assumptions of the condensation calculation itself (gas-minimisation setup, molecule set, pressure) — that belongs in simulation.py, not post-processing You want to expand the thermochemical or stellar abundance databases (s4adding_data.py) rather than clean an existing simulation result The raw abundance curves are already smooth and the 50% condensation temperatures reproduce benchmark values — unnecessary cleaning could distort the curves

skills.description: Use when you need equilibrium condensation sequences or 50% condensation temperatures (Tc) of rock-forming elements (Al, Ti, Ca, Mg, Fe, Si) for a given stellar abundance pattern and disk pressure, e.g. reproducing Table 2 benchmarks at p = 1e-4 bar.
skills.name: condensation-sequence-simulation
skills.search_text: condensation-sequence-simulation Use when you need equilibrium condensation sequences or 50% condensation temperatures (Tc) of rock-forming elements (Al, Ti, Ca, Mg, Fe, Si) for a given stellar abundance pattern and disk pressure, e.g. reproducing Table 2 benchmarks at p = 1e-4 bar. Only gas-phase chemistry is needed — the TEA code is cited as an open-source alternative but ECCOplanets is built for condensation with pure-condensate species Solid-solution minerals are required — the first release only considers pure minerals Simulations on very incomplete abundance data sets (e.g. if Al, Ca, Mg, Si, or O data is not reported) may be insensible Simulates the T-p-dependent equilibrium condensation sequence of a protoplanetary disk by Gibbs free energy minimisation with a trust-region solver, using ECCOplanets to compute element and molecule abundances as a function of temperature and derive 50% condensation temperatures of planet-building elements. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202244850
skills.summary: Simulates the T-p-dependent equilibrium condensation sequence of a protoplanetary disk by Gibbs free energy minimisation with a trust-region solver, using ECCOplanets to compute element and molecule abundances as a function of temperature and derive 50% condensation temperatures of planet-building elements.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only gas-phase chemistry is needed — the TEA code is cited as an open-source alternative but ECCOplanets is built for condensation with pure-condensate species Solid-solution minerals are required — the first release only considers pure minerals Simulations on very incomplete abundance data sets (e.g. if Al, Ca, Mg, Si, or O data is not reported) may be insensible

skills.description: Use when a T-p-dependent condensation simulation (Gibbs minimisation over gas + pure-condensate species) has been run for a stellar abundance pattern at a fixed pressure (e.g. 1e-4 bar) and you need to extract and validate per-element condensation temperatures against literature benchmarks.
skills.name: condensation-temperature-derivation
skills.search_text: condensation-temperature-derivation Use when a T-p-dependent condensation simulation (Gibbs minimisation over gas + pure-condensate species) has been run for a stellar abundance pattern at a fixed pressure (e.g. 1e-4 bar) and you need to extract and validate per-element condensation temperatures against literature benchmarks. The input chemistry is gas-phase only (e.g. hot-atmosphere equilibrium with TEA-style codes) — no condensate 50% point exists to extract Simulations require solid-solution minerals rather than pure minerals — the ECCOplanets code considers only pure minerals at present The stellar abundance pattern is highly incomplete for key planet-building elements (Al, Ca, Mg, Si, O data missing) — running such simulations is flagged as scientifically unsound in the README http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Derive 50%-condensation temperatures of common rocky species (corundum, perovskite, gehlenite, spinel, anorthite, iron, forsterite, diopside, enstatite) from an ECCOplanets Gibbs free energy minimisation condensation simulation, and benchmark them against the Lodders2003a Condor-code values. It turns raw temperature-resolved molar abundance curves into per-element condensation temperatures for a given pressure and stellar abundance pattern. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202244850
skills.summary: Derive 50%-condensation temperatures of common rocky species (corundum, perovskite, gehlenite, spinel, anorthite, iron, forsterite, diopside, enstatite) from an ECCOplanets Gibbs free energy minimisation condensation simulation, and benchmark them against the Lodders2003a Condor-code values. It turns raw temperature-resolved molar abundance curves into per-element condensation temperatures for a given pressure and stellar abundance pattern.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input chemistry is gas-phase only (e.g. hot-atmosphere equilibrium with TEA-style codes) — no condensate 50% point exists to extract Simulations require solid-solution minerals rather than pure minerals — the ECCOplanets code considers only pure minerals at present The stellar abundance pattern is highly incomplete for key planet-building elements (Al, Ca, Mg, Si, O data missing) — running such simulations is flagged as scientifically unsound in the README

skills.description: Use when you have run (or need to run) an ECCOplanets equilibrium condensation simulation and must convert element/molecule abundance-vs-temperature curves into per-element 50% condensation temperatures for validation or composition analysis.
skills.name: condensation-temperature-extraction
skills.search_text: condensation-temperature-extraction Use when you have run (or need to run) an ECCOplanets equilibrium condensation simulation and must convert element/molecule abundance-vs-temperature curves into per-element 50% condensation temperatures for validation or composition analysis. The goal is planet bulk composition or devolatilisation relative to the host star (s3planet_composition.py / planet class), not per-element condensation temperature extraction. The simulation is gas-phase only (e.g. the TEA code mentioned in the paper) — no condensation occurs, so no 50% condensation point exists. The stellar abundance pattern is too incomplete for condensation chemistry (e.g. Al, Ca, Mg, Si, or O data not reported), as the README warns against running simulations on such data. http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Extracts 50% condensation temperatures (Tc) of rock-forming elements from ECCOplanets Gibbs-free-energy-minimisation condensation simulations by post-processing molecule-vs-temperature abundance curves, and validates them against literature benchmark values within ±5 K. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202244850
skills.summary: Extracts 50% condensation temperatures (Tc) of rock-forming elements from ECCOplanets Gibbs-free-energy-minimisation condensation simulations by post-processing molecule-vs-temperature abundance curves, and validates them against literature benchmark values within ±5 K.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is planet bulk composition or devolatilisation relative to the host star (s3planet_composition.py / planet class), not per-element condensation temperature extraction. The simulation is gas-phase only (e.g. the TEA code mentioned in the paper) — no condensation occurs, so no 50% condensation point exists. The stellar abundance pattern is too incomplete for condensation chemistry (e.g. Al, Ca, Mg, Si, or O data not reported), as the README warns against running simulations on such data.

skills.description: Use when you need to determine how equilibrium condensation temperatures of rock-forming elements depend on disk pressure (e.g. testing whether element volatility defined at Solar System pressure applies to other disks), or to reproduce a ∆Tc vs. pressure sensitivity table.
skills.name: condensation-temperature-pressure-sensitivity-analysis
skills.search_text: condensation-temperature-pressure-sensitivity-analysis Use when you need to determine how equilibrium condensation temperatures of rock-forming elements depend on disk pressure (e.g. testing whether element volatility defined at Solar System pressure applies to other disks), or to reproduce a ∆Tc vs. pressure sensitivity table. The question concerns abundance-pattern sensitivity (e.g. C/O variation from 0.1 to 0.7 giving ∆Tc ≈ −100 K) or metallicity ([M/H] −0.3 to 0.4 giving ∆Tc ≈ +100 K) rather than disk pressure — vary those parameters instead. You need full planet bulk compositions, devolatilisation, or feeding-zone (FZ) model outputs — use the s3planet_composition.py workflow, not a Tc-vs-pressure sweep. Your code cannot handle condensed phases (e.g. gas-phase-only codes like TEA) — condensation temperatures of rock-forming elements require Gibbs minimisation over solid species. http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Quantifies how the 50% condensation temperatures (Tc) of major planet-building elements (Mg, Si, Fe, Al, Ca, Na, Ni) shift with protoplanetary disk pressure, using the ECCOplanets Gibbs free energy minimisation code over logarithmically spaced pressures from 1e-6 to 0.1 bar to recover a mean ∆Tc ≈ +350 K. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202244850
skills.summary: Quantifies how the 50% condensation temperatures (Tc) of major planet-building elements (Mg, Si, Fe, Al, Ca, Na, Ni) shift with protoplanetary disk pressure, using the ECCOplanets Gibbs free energy minimisation code over logarithmically spaced pressures from 1e-6 to 0.1 bar to recover a mean ∆Tc ≈ +350 K.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The question concerns abundance-pattern sensitivity (e.g. C/O variation from 0.1 to 0.7 giving ∆Tc ≈ −100 K) or metallicity ([M/H] −0.3 to 0.4 giving ∆Tc ≈ +100 K) rather than disk pressure — vary those parameters instead. You need full planet bulk compositions, devolatilisation, or feeding-zone (FZ) model outputs — use the s3planet_composition.py workflow, not a Tc-vs-pressure sweep. Your code cannot handle condensed phases (e.g. gas-phase-only codes like TEA) — condensation temperatures of rock-forming elements require Gibbs minimisation over solid species.

skills.description: Use when solving hyperbolic conservative systems (e.g. 1D SRHD) with shock-capturing schemes, where the spatial flux term must remain in conservative form while variables are evolved in primitive form.
skills.name: conservative-variable-flux-formulation
skills.search_text: conservative-variable-flux-formulation Use when solving hyperbolic conservative systems (e.g. 1D SRHD) with shock-capturing schemes, where the spatial flux term must remain in conservative form while variables are evolved in primitive form. The system is not hyperbolic or cannot be written in conservative form ∂q/∂t+∂f/∂x=S (e.g. purely non-conservative or source-dominated formulations), since the HLL jump structure and Rankine-Hugoniot argument depend on it The problem has no discontinuities and shock-capturing/conservative fluxes are unnecessary, e.g. a smooth static consistency check alone http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Formulate a hyperbolic PDE system as conservative charges q=(D,Sx,τ) and fluxes f as explicit functions of primitive variables u=(p,v,n), and keep the spatial discretization in conservative finite-volume form (HLL flux) so entropy and Rankine-Hugoniot jump conditions are not violated. astronomy/v1 10.1371/journal.pone.0195494
skills.summary: Formulate a hyperbolic PDE system as conservative charges q=(D,Sx,τ) and fluxes f as explicit functions of primitive variables u=(p,v,n), and keep the spatial discretization in conservative finite-volume form (HLL flux) so entropy and Rankine-Hugoniot jump conditions are not violated.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The system is not hyperbolic or cannot be written in conservative form ∂q/∂t+∂f/∂x=S (e.g. purely non-conservative or source-dominated formulations), since the HLL jump structure and Rankine-Hugoniot argument depend on it The problem has no discontinuities and shock-capturing/conservative fluxes are unnecessary, e.g. a smooth static consistency check alone

When the goal is only to quantify the flux contamination itself (flux fractions, CROWDSAP/FLFRCSAP metrics, heatmaps/pie charts) rather than attribute the signal — that is steps (1)-(2) of TESS-cont, not the dilution/filtering step When the measured transit depth is NOT corrected for dilution (e.g. raw SAP-like photometry) — running with dilution_corr: True would wrongly rescale the depth When TESS photometry alone is insufficient and high-spatial-resolution follow-up (ground-based photometry/spectroscopy) is already available to directly confirm or discard contaminant origins Step (3) of TESS-cont: given the per-source flux fractions of Gaia DR2/DR3 contaminants inside the TESS photometric aperture, compute the transit depth each nearby star would need to produce the observed signal and discard sources whose implied depth is unphysical (>=100%). astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202451656

skills.description: Use when two or more bodies follow Keplerian orbits around a central mass with intersecting orbits, and you need analytic soonest-collision times or a fast collision-detection schedule rather than brute-force time stepping.
skills.name: continued-fraction-period-ratio-analysis
skills.search_text: continued-fraction-period-ratio-analysis Use when two or more bodies follow Keplerian orbits around a central mass with intersecting orbits, and you need analytic soonest-collision times or a fast collision-detection schedule rather than brute-force time stepping. The system requires full gravitational N-body interaction treatment — the method treats gravitational interactions only as gravitational scattering or secular perturbation, at the cost of reducing the time-step or accuracy Orbits are large and dense such that collisions dominate the dynamics (e.g. N >= 10^8 for Solar-System-like systems); large time jumps pay off only when collisions are rare Bodies are on non-intersecting Kepler orbits, so no lattice/parallel-lines collision geometry exists http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 Analytic method that computes the time of collision between bodies on intersecting Kepler orbits by reducing the problem to finding the grid point between two parallel lines closest to the origin, solved via the continued fraction of the ratio of the orbital periods. It enables large jumps in time from collision to collision instead of small-step integration. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202243754
skills.summary: Analytic method that computes the time of collision between bodies on intersecting Kepler orbits by reducing the problem to finding the grid point between two parallel lines closest to the origin, solved via the continued fraction of the ratio of the orbital periods. It enables large jumps in time from collision to collision instead of small-step integration.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The system requires full gravitational N-body interaction treatment — the method treats gravitational interactions only as gravitational scattering or secular perturbation, at the cost of reducing the time-step or accuracy Orbits are large and dense such that collisions dominate the dynamics (e.g. N >= 10^8 for Solar-System-like systems); large time jumps pay off only when collisions are rare Bodies are on non-intersecting Kepler orbits, so no lattice/parallel-lines collision geometry exists

skills.description: Use when you need to show a discrete recurrent network (GRU) is the Euler discretisation of a continuous-time ODE system, or to inspect the -h(t) exponential-decay term governing hidden-state dynamics.
skills.name: continuous-time-gru-vector-field-implementation
skills.search_text: continuous-time-gru-vector-field-implementation Use when you need to show a discrete recurrent network (GRU) is the Euler discretisation of a continuous-time ODE system, or to inspect the -h(t) exponential-decay term governing hidden-state dynamics. When the input is an irregularly sampled time series needing a true continuous-time model — use a neural CDE solved with an adaptive solver (e.g. Tsit5) rather than a unit-step Euler discretisation of a GRU. When the goal is training rather than equivalence verification — machine-precision Euler matching is a validation exercise, not a modelling improvement over the discrete GRU. Implements the continuous-time GRU of Example 3.14 — gating variables i(t), r(t), n(t) with hidden-state ODE dh/dt = (1-i(t))*(n(t)-h(t)) — as a diffrax.ODETerm in JAX, then verifies that an explicit Euler discretisation with unit step size reproduces the standard discrete GRU recurrence to machine precision. astronomy/v1 10.48550/arxiv.2202.02435
skills.summary: Implements the continuous-time GRU of Example 3.14 — gating variables i(t), r(t), n(t) with hidden-state ODE dh/dt = (1-i(t))*(n(t)-h(t)) — as a diffrax.ODETerm in JAX, then verifies that an explicit Euler discretisation with unit step size reproduces the standard discrete GRU recurrence to machine precision.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is an irregularly sampled time series needing a true continuous-time model — use a neural CDE solved with an adaptive solver (e.g. Tsit5) rather than a unit-step Euler discretisation of a GRU. When the goal is training rather than equivalence verification — machine-precision Euler matching is a validation exercise, not a modelling improvement over the discrete GRU.

skills.description: Use when automating radio-synthesis imaging (e.g. chimenea/CASA Clean) and you must decide when iterative re-Cleaning has converged, since estimating an RMS threshold requires an image to sample.
skills.name: convergence-criterion-tuning-for-iterative-imaging
skills.search_text: convergence-criterion-tuning-for-iterative-imaging Use when automating radio-synthesis imaging (e.g. chimenea/CASA Clean) and you must decide when iterative re-Cleaning has converged, since estimating an RMS threshold requires an image to sample. skills.search_text: cross-backend-consistency-comparison Use when a GAMBIT observable can be computed by multiple interchangeable backends and you need to verify that different external codes agree on the same pinned model point, rather than relying on a single backend's output. Only one backend implementing the observable is available or buildable — no cross-check is possible The goal is a global statistical scan over parameter space rather than a fixed benchmark-point code comparison The observable is computed natively by a GAMBIT module (e.g. DarkBit's own gamma-ray yield) with no external backend alternative http://edamontology.org/topic_3452 Compute the same observable (e.g. the dark matter relic density for a shared MSSM7 benchmark point) through two alternative GAMBIT backends — DarkSUSY and micrOMEGAs 4.1 — and quantify their relative difference as a cross-code consistency check, mirroring DarkBit's quantitative comparison of the two main dark matter codes. astronomy/v1 10.1140/epjc/s10052-017-5155-4
skills.summary: Compute the same observable (e.g. the dark matter relic density for a shared MSSM7 benchmark point) through two alternative GAMBIT backends — DarkSUSY and micrOMEGAs 4.1 — and quantify their relative difference as a cross-code consistency check, mirroring DarkBit's quantitative comparison of the two main dark matter codes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one backend implementing the observable is available or buildable — no cross-check is possible The goal is a global statistical scan over parameter space rather than a fixed benchmark-point code comparison The observable is computed natively by a GAMBIT module (e.g. DarkBit's own gamma-ray yield) with no external backend alternative

skills.description: Use when a benchmark problem has run through two independent solvers (e.g., Dedalus 2048^2 spectral modes vs. Athena finite-volume) and you must quantify how resolution governs accuracy against unphysical secondary instabilities.
skills.name: cross-code-field-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-code-field-comparison Use when a benchmark problem has run through two independent solvers (e.g., Dedalus 2048^2 spectral modes vs. Athena finite-volume) and you must quantify how resolution governs accuracy against unphysical secondary instabilities. The goal is a single-code convergence study with no independent reference solver, so no cross-code field alignment is possible Only scalar or time-series diagnostics (e.g., growth rates, eigenvalues) are to be compared, rather than full 2D field states The problem's solutions are non-smooth enough that spectral methods are inappropriate, so the resolution-gap comparison would not be meaningful Quantifies field-level agreement between a spectral-method code (Dedalus) and a finite-volume reference code (Athena) on a shared hydrodynamic benchmark, here the 2D Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, by aligning late-time snapshots at matched physical times and computing relative differences in vorticity/density fields. astronomy/v1 10.1103/physrevresearch.2.023068
skills.summary: Quantifies field-level agreement between a spectral-method code (Dedalus) and a finite-volume reference code (Athena) on a shared hydrodynamic benchmark, here the 2D Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, by aligning late-time snapshots at matched physical times and computing relative differences in vorticity/density fields.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a single-code convergence study with no independent reference solver, so no cross-code field alignment is possible Only scalar or time-series diagnostics (e.g., growth rates, eigenvalues) are to be compared, rather than full 2D field states The problem's solutions are non-smooth enough that spectral methods are inappropriate, so the resolution-gap comparison would not be meaningful

skills.description: Use when two or more N-body codes must be validated against each other via relative power spectra P_codeA/P_codeB, especially when diagnosing force-solver differences (multipole order, randomised displacements) at early vs late redshifts.
skills.name: cross-code-n-body-power-spectrum-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-code-n-body-power-spectrum-comparison Use when two or more N-body codes must be validated against each other via relative power spectra P_codeA/P_codeB, especially when diagnosing force-solver differences (multipole order, randomised displacements) at early vs late redshifts. Validating a single code against the linear theory of an Einstein-Boltzmann solver such as CLASS rather than against another N-body code Benchmarking runtime performance or scaling rather than spectral accuracy — CONCEPT is several times faster than GADGET-2 only for k_Nyquist < 5 Mpc/h and slower at higher resolution Cases where initial conditions are not shared between the codes, since ratios then conflate IC differences with force-solver differences http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 http://edamontology.org/topic_3452 Compares matter power spectra from CONCEPT 1.0 and GADGET-4 (TreePM and FMM-PM solvers) on identical initial conditions in a 512 Mpc/h box with N=1024^3 particles, quantifying code-to-code agreement and diagnosing solver-specific discrepancies such as the early-time (z=10) FMM-PM power suppression. astronomy/v1 10.1093/mnras/stac568
skills.summary: Compares matter power spectra from CONCEPT 1.0 and GADGET-4 (TreePM and FMM-PM solvers) on identical initial conditions in a 512 Mpc/h box with N=1024^3 particles, quantifying code-to-code agreement and diagnosing solver-specific discrepancies such as the early-time (z=10) FMM-PM power suppression.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Validating a single code against the linear theory of an Einstein-Boltzmann solver such as CLASS rather than against another N-body code Benchmarking runtime performance or scaling rather than spectral accuracy — CONCEPT is several times faster than GADGET-2 only for k_Nyquist < 5 Mpc/h and slower at higher resolution Cases where initial conditions are not shared between the codes, since ratios then conflate IC differences with force-solver differences

skills.description: Use when a custom octree traversal must reproduce FleCSPH's neighbor lists: reference data from a sodtube/hydro generator is available, particles are inserted into the FleCSI octree, and per-particle neighbor lists must be cross-checked entry-by-entry.
skills.name: cross-code-neighbor-list-verification
skills.search_text: cross-code-neighbor-list-verification Use when a custom octree traversal must reproduce FleCSPH's neighbor lists: reference data from a sodtube/hydro generator is available, particles are inserted into the FleCSI octree, and per-particle neighbor lists must be cross-checked entry-by-entry. The goal is to validate FMM gravitational forces or shock-physics results (Sedov, Noh) rather than SPH neighbor-list construction — this skill only checks neighbor-list equivalence. The problem fits on a single rank, so no non-local tree nodes are encountered and the asynchronous MPI request path cannot be exercised. The tree under test is FleCSPH's own FleCSI octree; there is no second, independent implementation to compare against. Validates an independently implemented distributed octree neighbor-list construction against FleCSPH's own FleCSI octree by comparing exported neighbor lists entry-by-entry on identical particles and parameter files (e.g. the 1D Sod shock tube). astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.softx.2020.100602
skills.summary: Validates an independently implemented distributed octree neighbor-list construction against FleCSPH's own FleCSI octree by comparing exported neighbor lists entry-by-entry on identical particles and parameter files (e.g. the 1D Sod shock tube).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to validate FMM gravitational forces or shock-physics results (Sedov, Noh) rather than SPH neighbor-list construction — this skill only checks neighbor-list equivalence. The problem fits on a single rank, so no non-local tree nodes are encountered and the asynchronous MPI request path cannot be exercised. The tree under test is FleCSPH's own FleCSI octree; there is no second, independent implementation to compare against.

skills.description: Use when two codes have produced radial profiles (x_HII, x_HeII, x_HeIII, T) for the same well-posed problem and you must quantify agreement, e.g. validating rabacus against Cloudy 13.03 reference profiles.
skills.name: cross-code-profile-interpolation-and-difference-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-code-profile-interpolation-and-difference-analysis Use when two codes have produced radial profiles (x_HII, x_HeII, x_HeIII, T) for the same well-posed problem and you must quantify agreement, e.g. validating rabacus against Cloudy 13.03 reference profiles. The problem is not one of rabacus's supported geometries — a semi-infinite slab in an isotropic background, a spherically symmetric gas with a point source at the center, or a spherically symmetric gas in an isotropic background. You need non-equilibrium or metal-line-cooling physics: the paper states these solvers are planned future improvements and not yet included. The two codes were not run on the same physical setup (source spectrum, band truncation, luminosity, and temperature-evolution toggle must match), making pointwise differences meaningless. http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 A validation skill that compares radial ionization-fraction and temperature profiles from two radiative-transfer codes (e.g. rabacus and Cloudy 13.03) by interpolating one solver's outputs onto the other's radial grid and computing pointwise relative differences, as done for the Iliev et al. (2006) Test 2 sphere. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2015.01.004
skills.summary: A validation skill that compares radial ionization-fraction and temperature profiles from two radiative-transfer codes (e.g. rabacus and Cloudy 13.03) by interpolating one solver's outputs onto the other's radial grid and computing pointwise relative differences, as done for the Iliev et al. (2006) Test 2 sphere.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The problem is not one of rabacus's supported geometries — a semi-infinite slab in an isotropic background, a spherically symmetric gas with a point source at the center, or a spherically symmetric gas in an isotropic background. You need non-equilibrium or metal-line-cooling physics: the paper states these solvers are planned future improvements and not yet included. The two codes were not run on the same physical setup (source spectrum, band truncation, luminosity, and temperature-evolution toggle must match), making pointwise differences meaningless.

skills.description: Use when validating a new forward-modelling tool against an established code: you need a single-realization runtime ratio plus fractional-agreement of model outputs (e.g. rotation/dispersion curves) on matched synthetic observations.
skills.name: cross-code-runtime-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-code-runtime-benchmarking Use when validating a new forward-modelling tool against an established code: you need a single-realization runtime ratio plus fractional-agreement of model outputs (e.g. rotation/dispersion curves) on matched synthetic observations. You need to benchmark on real observational IFU data rather than synthetic mock observations with a controlled, identical PSF and sky-orientation across codes The codes cannot be given the same fiducial mass model or produce comparable outputs (e.g. one lacks dispersion-curve reconstruction), making fractional-agreement computation ill-defined The system is not a rotationally supported axisymmetric disk galaxy (V/sigma_0 >~ 2) with a well-defined kinematic axis, which is outside the mass-model scope both codes share http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Benchmark a new parametric modelling code (RotCurves) against an established reference code (dysmalpy) by (a) timing single realizations and (b) quantifying agreement of mock-observed rotation and dispersion curves under identical sky-orientation and PSF conditions. astronomy/v1 10.1093/mnras/stag134
skills.summary: Benchmark a new parametric modelling code (RotCurves) against an established reference code (dysmalpy) by (a) timing single realizations and (b) quantifying agreement of mock-observed rotation and dispersion curves under identical sky-orientation and PSF conditions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to benchmark on real observational IFU data rather than synthetic mock observations with a controlled, identical PSF and sky-orientation across codes The codes cannot be given the same fiducial mass model or produce comparable outputs (e.g. one lacks dispersion-curve reconstruction), making fractional-agreement computation ill-defined The system is not a rotationally supported axisymmetric disk galaxy (V/sigma_0 >~ 2) with a well-defined kinematic axis, which is outside the mass-model scope both codes share

skills.description: Use when two simulation codes' power spectra are available as |code_A/code_B − 1| versus k curves and you need to locate the wavenumber where they diverge beyond a threshold (e.g. 1‰) and determine whether that scale is resolution-dependent.
skills.name: cross-code-simulation-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-code-simulation-comparison Use when two simulation codes' power spectra are available as |code_A/code_B − 1| versus k curves and you need to locate the wavenumber where they diverge beyond a threshold (e.g. 1‰) and determine whether that scale is resolution-dependent. You need absolute power spectrum amplitudes or cosmological parameter fits rather than code-to-code relative agreement Only a single box size is available — the resolution-independence test requires comparing k_div × L_box / (24 × 2π) across at least two L_box values The comparison involves codes other than CONCEPT and GADGET without deposited |code_A/code_B − 1| curves in the same format http://edamontology.org/topic_3452 Quantify agreement between CONCEPT 1.0 and GADGET-2 cosmological N-body simulations by analyzing their relative power spectrum |CONCEPT/GADGET-2 − 1| versus wavenumber k, extracting the divergence wavenumber k_div where deviation first exceeds a 1‰ (0.001) threshold and testing whether it scales with simulation resolution (k_div ≈ 24 × 2π/L_box) rather than an absolute scale. astronomy/v1 10.1093/mnras/stac568
skills.summary: Quantify agreement between CONCEPT 1.0 and GADGET-2 cosmological N-body simulations by analyzing their relative power spectrum |CONCEPT/GADGET-2 − 1| versus wavenumber k, extracting the divergence wavenumber k_div where deviation first exceeds a 1‰ (0.001) threshold and testing whether it scales with simulation resolution (k_div ≈ 24 × 2π/L_box) rather than an absolute scale.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need absolute power spectrum amplitudes or cosmological parameter fits rather than code-to-code relative agreement Only a single box size is available — the resolution-independence test requires comparing k_div × L_box / (24 × 2π) across at least two L_box values The comparison involves codes other than CONCEPT and GADGET without deposited |code_A/code_B − 1| curves in the same format

skills.description: Use when a new linear perturbation solver's P(k) or CMB spectra must be validated against a benchmark code like CLASS, requiring grid alignment via interpolation and relative/absolute residual quantification.
skills.name: cross-code-spectra-interpolation-and-residual-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-code-spectra-interpolation-and-residual-analysis Use when a new linear perturbation solver's P(k) or CMB spectra must be validated against a benchmark code like CLASS, requiring grid alignment via interpolation and relative/absolute residual quantification. When comparing codes whose cosmological parameter sets or gauge choices differ (e.g. different gauge or recombination treatment) — residuals would conflate physical with numerical differences When the goal is accuracy benchmarking of a single solver's convergence (a work-precision diagram against a low-tolerance reference solution is the appropriate method instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_3360 Validates an Einstein-Boltzmann solver (SymBoltz) against an established reference code (CLASS) by comparing matter power spectrum P(k) and CMB D_l spectra (TT/TE/EE), interpolating one code's output onto the other's grid and computing residual statistics to quantify agreement (target ~0.1%). astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202557450
skills.summary: Validates an Einstein-Boltzmann solver (SymBoltz) against an established reference code (CLASS) by comparing matter power spectrum P(k) and CMB D_l spectra (TT/TE/EE), interpolating one code's output onto the other's grid and computing residual statistics to quantify agreement (target ~0.1%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When comparing codes whose cosmological parameter sets or gauge choices differ (e.g. different gauge or recombination treatment) — residuals would conflate physical with numerical differences When the goal is accuracy benchmarking of a single solver's convergence (a work-precision diagram against a low-tolerance reference solution is the appropriate method instead)

skills.description: Use when a newly computed dN/dE photon yield table for dark matter annihilation final states must be validated against established codes, or when quantitatively comparing dark matter codes' indirect-detection outputs.
skills.name: cross-code-yield-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-code-yield-comparison Use when a newly computed dN/dE photon yield table for dark matter annihilation final states must be validated against established codes, or when quantitatively comparing dark matter codes' indirect-detection outputs. The analysis concerns direct detection likelihoods (spin-independent/spin-dependent scattering) rather than gamma-ray photon yields No independent reference code (DarkSUSY or micrOMEGAs) is available or interfaced, so no external cross-check can be performed The model's annihilation involves few or exotic final states where the reference codes lack tabulated branching yields, so a meaningful comparison is impossible Validates a dark-matter code's gamma-ray yield tables by cross-checking them against yields computed with independent reference codes (DarkSUSY and micrOMEGAs), mirroring the DarkBit paper's quantitative dark-matter-code comparison. astronomy/v1 10.1140/epjc/s10052-017-5155-4
skills.summary: Validates a dark-matter code's gamma-ray yield tables by cross-checking them against yields computed with independent reference codes (DarkSUSY and micrOMEGAs), mirroring the DarkBit paper's quantitative dark-matter-code comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis concerns direct detection likelihoods (spin-independent/spin-dependent scattering) rather than gamma-ray photon yields No independent reference code (DarkSUSY or micrOMEGAs) is available or interfaced, so no external cross-check can be performed The model's annihilation involves few or exotic final states where the reference codes lack tabulated branching yields, so a meaningful comparison is impossible

skills.description: Use when you have ranked cross-correlation peak heights (v1, v2) from an autoz-style matcher and need to convert them into discrete match-quality classes (QOP1–QOP6) or flag matches needing manual merging.
skills.name: cross-correlation-peak-quality-assignment
skills.search_text: cross-correlation-peak-quality-assignment Use when you have ranked cross-correlation peak heights (v1, v2) from an autoz-style matcher and need to convert them into discrete match-quality classes (QOP1–QOP6) or flag matches needing manual merging. Spectra with only one correlation peak handled by a different path — apply the special normalisation factor of 1, not the standard FOM peak-ratio logic Manual redshifting tasks where the user cycles automatic results, compares templates manually, or marks spectral features instead of relying on automatic QOPs Redshift fitting against templates or instruments outside the autoz/Marz normalisation scheme, where peak heights are not autoz-style normalised Assigns a suggested quality operator (QOP) to automatic spectral matches by computing Marz's Figure of Merit (FOM = (v1 - 2.5)^0.75 * v1/v2) from the two highest normalised cross-correlation peak heights, then thresholding FOM into QOP classes. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2016.03.001
skills.summary: Assigns a suggested quality operator (QOP) to automatic spectral matches by computing Marz's Figure of Merit (FOM = (v1 - 2.5)^0.75 * v1/v2) from the two highest normalised cross-correlation peak heights, then thresholding FOM into QOP classes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra with only one correlation peak handled by a different path — apply the special normalisation factor of 1, not the standard FOM peak-ratio logic Manual redshifting tasks where the user cycles automatic results, compares templates manually, or marks spectral features instead of relying on automatic QOPs Redshift fitting against templates or instruments outside the autoz/Marz normalisation scheme, where peak heights are not autoz-style normalised

skills.description: Use when comparing storage codecs (e.g. FITS Rice vs HDF5 LZF_SS vs bitshuffle) on large binary-table or image data files, and you need per-codec compression ratio, compression time, and read time with lossless round-trip verification.
skills.name: cross-format-storage-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-format-storage-comparison Use when comparing storage codecs (e.g. FITS Rice vs HDF5 LZF_SS vs bitshuffle) on large binary-table or image data files, and you need per-codec compression ratio, compression time, and read time with lossless round-trip verification. Evaluating lossy compression algorithms — the underlying study explicitly did not compare lossy compression methods, so this skill only supports lossless codecs Input files are small or dominated by headers/metadata rather than large typed binary arrays, where compression ratios and codec throughput differences are not meaningful Data contain correlations spanning fewer than 24 elements — bitshuffle relies on neighbouring-element correlation, so ratios will be poor http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Benchmarking compression ratio and wall-clock time of FITS Rice (FPACK -table) against HDF5 LZF_SS and bitshuffle codecs on large astronomical binary-table files, using fits2hdf for FITS-to-HDF5 conversion and lossless round-trip validation. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2015.05.001
skills.summary: Benchmarking compression ratio and wall-clock time of FITS Rice (FPACK -table) against HDF5 LZF_SS and bitshuffle codecs on large astronomical binary-table files, using fits2hdf for FITS-to-HDF5 conversion and lossless round-trip validation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating lossy compression algorithms — the underlying study explicitly did not compare lossy compression methods, so this skill only supports lossless codecs Input files are small or dominated by headers/metadata rather than large typed binary arrays, where compression ratios and codec throughput differences are not meaningful Data contain correlations spanning fewer than 24 elements — bitshuffle relies on neighbouring-element correlation, so ratios will be poor

skills.description: Use when building or testing an in-memory store that passes calculation results between sequential pipeline modules, especially when values must be keyed by (section, name) pairs and retrieved via typed getters.
skills.name: cross-module-data-passing-testing
skills.search_text: cross-module-data-passing-testing Use when building or testing an in-memory store that passes calculation results between sequential pipeline modules, especially when values must be keyed by (section, name) pairs and retrieved via typed getters. When data must be shared across processes or persisted to disk — the DataBlock is an in-memory container passed module to module, not a storage format When values of mixed types must be stored under the same (section, name) key — replacement must always be with the same type When keys need to preserve case or be non-string types — keys must be strings and are always treated as lower-case Implements and tests a CosmoSIS-style DataBlock, an in-memory dictionary keyed by (section, name) string pairs that carries module calculation results between pipeline stages, with typed get/put access and type-preservation rules. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2015.05.005
skills.summary: Implements and tests a CosmoSIS-style DataBlock, an in-memory dictionary keyed by (section, name) string pairs that carries module calculation results between pipeline stages, with typed get/put access and type-preservation rules.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When data must be shared across processes or persisted to disk — the DataBlock is an in-memory container passed module to module, not a storage format When values of mixed types must be stored under the same (section, name) key — replacement must always be with the same type When keys need to preserve case or be non-string types — keys must be strings and are always treated as lower-case

skills.description: Use when analyzing multiple public IXPE level-2 event files and you need per-observation characterization of the instrumental background's off-axis radial distribution (slope alpha) for background modeling or subtraction.
skills.name: cross-observation-background-variability-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-observation-background-variability-analysis Use when analyzing multiple public IXPE level-2 event files and you need per-observation characterization of the instrumental background's off-axis radial distribution (slope alpha) for background modeling or subtraction. The analysis region is source-dominated rather than background-dominated — the radial alpha fit requires background-only event samples. The goal is forward simulation of IXPE observations rather than characterizing the background in real archived observations. The data are from a different mission — ixpeobssim is IXPE-specific, and adapting it to other missions requires modifying the underlying implementation. Quantifies how the IXPE instrumental background varies across observations by fitting the off-axis radial distribution of background-dominated events with a linear radial-dependence model and extracting the fitted slope alpha per observation. It grounds background modeling in the actual radiation-environment variability of low-Earth orbit rather than assuming a uniform background. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.softx.2022.101194
skills.summary: Quantifies how the IXPE instrumental background varies across observations by fitting the off-axis radial distribution of background-dominated events with a linear radial-dependence model and extracting the fitted slope alpha per observation. It grounds background modeling in the actual radiation-environment variability of low-Earth orbit rather than assuming a uniform background.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis region is source-dominated rather than background-dominated — the radial alpha fit requires background-only event samples. The goal is forward simulation of IXPE observations rather than characterizing the background in real archived observations. The data are from a different mission — ixpeobssim is IXPE-specific, and adapting it to other missions requires modifying the underlying implementation.

skills.description: Use when parallelised MCMC chains from different samplers (e.g. emcee ensemble walkers vs. Metropolis–Hastings chains) must be compared for initialisation bias and a burn-in length must be justified numerically.
skills.name: cross-sampler-convergence-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-sampler-convergence-comparison Use when parallelised MCMC chains from different samplers (e.g. emcee ensemble walkers vs. Metropolis–Hastings chains) must be compared for initialisation bias and a burn-in length must be justified numerically. Only one sampler is being run and no cross-sampler comparison is needed — a single-chain convergence diagnostic suffices and the X̄_t vs sigma/sqrt(L) comparison adds no information. The likelihood is not the WMAP7 CMB posterior with six sampled cosmological parameters — the walkers ratio of 50 (walkers = 50 × n_parameters) and the calibrated 250-step burn-in were determined for that specific posterior and must be re-derived for other problems. The CosmoMC chains are still within their ~2000-step self-tuning/proposal-adaptation phase — such samples are not yet usable and would contaminate the burn-in estimate. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 A protocol for comparing burn-in / convergence behaviour of two MCMC samplers (CosmoHammer's emcee ensemble sampler vs. the Metropolis–Hastings sampler of fine-tuned CosmoMC) by tracking the ensemble mean sequential step X̄_t against the predicted standard error sigma/sqrt(L), yielding a common burn-in length of 250 iterations despite different autocorrelation times. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.06.003
skills.summary: A protocol for comparing burn-in / convergence behaviour of two MCMC samplers (CosmoHammer's emcee ensemble sampler vs. the Metropolis–Hastings sampler of fine-tuned CosmoMC) by tracking the ensemble mean sequential step X̄_t against the predicted standard error sigma/sqrt(L), yielding a common burn-in length of 250 iterations despite different autocorrelation times.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one sampler is being run and no cross-sampler comparison is needed — a single-chain convergence diagnostic suffices and the X̄_t vs sigma/sqrt(L) comparison adds no information. The likelihood is not the WMAP7 CMB posterior with six sampled cosmological parameters — the walkers ratio of 50 (walkers = 50 × n_parameters) and the calibrated 250-step burn-in were determined for that specific posterior and must be re-derived for other problems. The CosmoMC chains are still within their ~2000-step self-tuning/proposal-adaptation phase — such samples are not yet usable and would contaminate the burn-in estimate.

skills.description: Use when a newly implemented MCMC sampler (e.g. DE-MC with N=2d chains, gamma=2.38/sqrt(2d)) must be validated by reproducing posterior percentiles of a high-dimensional Bayesian model against an independent long-run reference sampler like WinBUGS.
skills.name: cross-sampler-convergence-comparison-against-bugs-reference
skills.search_text: cross-sampler-convergence-comparison-against-bugs-reference Use when a newly implemented MCMC sampler (e.g. DE-MC with N=2d chains, gamma=2.38/sqrt(2d)) must be validated by reproducing posterior percentiles of a high-dimensional Bayesian model against an independent long-run reference sampler like WinBUGS. The model lives in a generalized linear model context where WinBUGS itself performs well with standard one-dimensional updates, making a cross-sampler benchmark redundant The initial chain population covers only a single modal region of a multimodal posterior — distant modes cannot be reached, so percentile agreement would be misleading No trustworthy long-run reference exists; comparing two unvalidated samplers does not establish convergence http://edamontology.org/topic_3489 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Validate a new MCMC sampler (e.g. DE-MC on a 43-parameter Theophylline nonlinear mixed-effects model) by comparing its posterior percentiles (P2.5/P50/P97.5) against a very long reference run from an independent sampler such as WinBUGS, within Monte Carlo error. astronomy/v1 10.1007/s11222-006-8769-1
skills.summary: Validate a new MCMC sampler (e.g. DE-MC on a 43-parameter Theophylline nonlinear mixed-effects model) by comparing its posterior percentiles (P2.5/P50/P97.5) against a very long reference run from an independent sampler such as WinBUGS, within Monte Carlo error.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model lives in a generalized linear model context where WinBUGS itself performs well with standard one-dimensional updates, making a cross-sampler benchmark redundant The initial chain population covers only a single modal region of a multimodal posterior — distant modes cannot be reached, so percentile agreement would be misleading No trustworthy long-run reference exists; comparing two unvalidated samplers does not establish convergence

skills.description: Use when a composite X-ray spectral model has been fitted in one framework and you need to confirm the posterior parameter estimates are reliable by benchmarking them against a blind reference fit (e.g. XSPEC with C-stat) or another software approach.
skills.name: cross-software-fit-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-software-fit-comparison Use when a composite X-ray spectral model has been fitted in one framework and you need to confirm the posterior parameter estimates are reliable by benchmarking them against a blind reference fit (e.g. XSPEC with C-stat) or another software approach. The input is not an OGIP-standard X-ray spectrum or the goal lies outside spectral fitting (jaxspec's scope is loading OGIP spectra, defining models from implemented components, and Bayesian parameter inference) You only need a quick chi-square point estimate without a Bayesian posterior; the article notes chi-square gives biased parameter estimates at low counts, so this comparison framework (Poisson/C-stat likelihood) would be unnecessary or misapplied A comprehensive background error budget requiring dispersion propagation is needed — the SubtractedBackground model accounts for observed counts without propagating any kind of dispersion http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Validates a Bayesian X-ray spectral fit by reproducing it in jaxspec (NUTS sampler under a Poisson/C-stat likelihood) and comparing posterior parameter estimates against an independent fit from an established framework such as XSPEC with C-stat, establishing equivalence of results and relative runtime. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202451736
skills.summary: Validates a Bayesian X-ray spectral fit by reproducing it in jaxspec (NUTS sampler under a Poisson/C-stat likelihood) and comparing posterior parameter estimates against an independent fit from an established framework such as XSPEC with C-stat, establishing equivalence of results and relative runtime.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not an OGIP-standard X-ray spectrum or the goal lies outside spectral fitting (jaxspec's scope is loading OGIP spectra, defining models from implemented components, and Bayesian parameter inference) You only need a quick chi-square point estimate without a Bayesian posterior; the article notes chi-square gives biased parameter estimates at low counts, so this comparison framework (Poisson/C-stat likelihood) would be unnecessary or misapplied A comprehensive background error budget requiring dispersion propagation is needed — the SubtractedBackground model accounts for observed counts without propagating any kind of dispersion

skills.description: Use when sampling a high-dimensional posterior (e.g. the 43-parameter Theophylline nonlinear mixed-effects model) via block updating, where full-vector DE-MC jumps mix poorly and per-block jumps with binomial crossover are needed.
skills.name: crossover-proposal-generation
skills.search_text: crossover-proposal-generation Use when sampling a high-dimensional posterior (e.g. the 43-parameter Theophylline nonlinear mixed-effects model) via block updating, where full-vector DE-MC jumps mix poorly and per-block jumps with binomial crossover are needed. The target posterior is low-dimensional or an uncorrelated full-vector update already mixes well — plain DE-MC without block partitioning is simpler (DE-MC core can be coded in about 10 lines). The initial chain population covers only a single modal region and distant modes exist — crossover/block updates will not reach far-away modes. A Gibbs sampler is possible because the conditional distribution of the parameter (e.g. γ) is available in closed form and easy to sample directly. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 Generates block-wise DE-MC proposals by combining a differential-evolution jump (difference of two randomly chosen chains, scaled by γ = 2.38/sqrt(2*d_b)) with binomial crossover so only a random subset of block components receives the jump, enabling lower-dimensional Metropolis updates within a high-dimensional posterior. astronomy/v1 10.1007/s11222-006-8769-1
skills.summary: Generates block-wise DE-MC proposals by combining a differential-evolution jump (difference of two randomly chosen chains, scaled by γ = 2.38/sqrt(2*d_b)) with binomial crossover so only a random subset of block components receives the jump, enabling lower-dimensional Metropolis updates within a high-dimensional posterior.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target posterior is low-dimensional or an uncorrelated full-vector update already mixes well — plain DE-MC without block partitioning is simpler (DE-MC core can be coded in about 10 lines). The initial chain population covers only a single modal region and distant modes exist — crossover/block updates will not reach far-away modes. A Gibbs sampler is possible because the conditional distribution of the parameter (e.g. γ) is available in closed form and easy to sample directly.

skills.description: Use when evaluating or tuning the jump scale gamma of Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DE-MC) on a multimodal target such as a two-component Normal mixture, where random walk Metropolis fails and RMSE of the posterior mean and acceptance fraction are the quality metrics.

skills.description: Use when solving PDEs with Dedalus on a periodic 2D Fourier domain where quadratic nonlinear products of fields (e.g. convective and Lorentz-force terms in compressible MHD) must be evaluated on a mode grid such as 4096x4096.
skills.name: dealiased-fourier-nonlinear-evaluation
skills.search_text: dealiased-fourier-nonlinear-evaluation Use when solving PDEs with Dedalus on a periodic 2D Fourier domain where quadratic nonlinear products of fields (e.g. convective and Lorentz-force terms in compressible MHD) must be evaluated on a mode grid such as 4096x4096. The problem is linear or contains no quadratic nonlinear products — the 3/2 truncation buys nothing and only wastes the extra grid points. The flow is high-Mach-number/shock-forming but no explicit diffusion or other regularization is planned — bare spectral evaluation will produce Gibbs ringing rather than resolved shocks. The domain is not periodic or the variables are not naturally represented in a Fourier basis — a different Dedalus basis (e.g. Chebyshev/Zernuke-style) than the 2D periodic Fourier setup is required. http://edamontology.org/topic_3361 Evaluate quadratic nonlinear terms on a spectral Fourier grid with 3/2 (two-thirds) dealiasing so that aliasing errors from products of modes are removed before each timestep of a Dedalus PDE solve. This is what lets Dedalus resolve sharp spectral features, e.g. the density shocks of the Orszag-Tang vortex, without Gibbs-contaminated nonlinear terms. astronomy/v1 10.1103/physrevresearch.2.023068
skills.summary: Evaluate quadratic nonlinear terms on a spectral Fourier grid with 3/2 (two-thirds) dealiasing so that aliasing errors from products of modes are removed before each timestep of a Dedalus PDE solve. This is what lets Dedalus resolve sharp spectral features, e.g. the density shocks of the Orszag-Tang vortex, without Gibbs-contaminated nonlinear terms.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The problem is linear or contains no quadratic nonlinear products — the 3/2 truncation buys nothing and only wastes the extra grid points. The flow is high-Mach-number/shock-forming but no explicit diffusion or other regularization is planned — bare spectral evaluation will produce Gibbs ringing rather than resolved shocks. skills.search_text: density-field-variance-evaluation Use when estimating halo number density dn/dM or effective halo bias b(z) from dark matter halo mass function models (Press-Schechter, Sheth-Tormen, Tinker, etc.) and you need sigma(M) at a fixed cosmology. The analysis requires only galaxy clustering statistics (2PCF/3PCF measurements) rather than halo mass function modelling — use CBL's catalogue-handling and correlation-function classes instead. The particle data has not yet been split into bound/unbound populations — run the Strawberry halo finder with the boosted-potential criterion first, otherwise the 'two populations' profiles are undefined The analysis goal is identifying haloes themselves (topology-based halo finding), not characterising the radial structure of already-labelled populations The data is an analytic or tabulated profile rather than discrete simulation particles, so a spherically averaged particle histogram is unnecessary Computes spherically averaged density profiles of particle populations (specifically Strawberry's bound vs unbound components, labelled via the boosted-potential saddle-point binding criterion) to contrast their radial extents. skills.search_text: dependency-graph-cascading-update-implementation Use when a parameterized scientific calculation must be re-run after changing one or more inputs and only the dependent quantities should be recomputed rather than the entire pipeline. The user's changed parameters invalidate the underlying transfer function itself (e.g. cosmology changes requiring new CAMB runs), so savings shrink toward full recomputation A one-off calculation where no parameters will be updated after initial computation — the dependency-tracking machinery adds overhead without benefit Quantities outside the tracked dependency graph (untracked cached state) need to be updated, since update() only deletes quantities it knows depend on the changed variables http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Implements hmf's cascading parameter-update mechanism, in which update() deletes only tracked quantities (power, sigma, growth, n_eff, fsigma, dndlnm, ngtm) that depend directly or transitively on a changed input, avoiding full recomputation. When interpreting individual disc structures or kinematics — the skill applies only to population-level sample statistics and flux-size scaling When the observable is continuum dust flux or dust disc size rather than 12CO flux/size; the reported factors (3.6, 1.3) are specific to CO observables When a computationally-expensive thermochemical treatment (e.g. DALI) is required per disc; the semi-analytical model is a fast alternative accurate only within a factor of three http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Quantifies how much larger a usable disc sample is when ALMA 12CO integrated fluxes, rather than CO-disc radii (sizes), are used as the selection observable. In the Zagaria et al. (2023) study this yielded sample increases of a factor 1.3 (Lupus) and 3.6 (Upper Sco). astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202346164
skills.summary: Quantifies how much larger a usable disc sample is when ALMA 12CO integrated fluxes, rather than CO-disc radii (sizes), are used as the selection observable. In the Zagaria et al. (2023) study this yielded sample increases of a factor 1.3 (Lupus) and 3.6 (Upper Sco).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When interpreting individual disc structures or kinematics — the skill applies only to population-level sample statistics and flux-size scaling When the observable is continuum dust flux or dust disc size rather than 12CO flux/size; the reported factors (3.6, 1.3) are specific to CO observables When a computationally-expensive thermochemical treatment (e.g. DALI) is required per disc; the semi-analytical model is a fast alternative accurate only within a factor of three

skills.description: Use when primordial deuterium (or lithium) abundance predictions from a BBN code must be compared under different nuclear-rate compilations (PRIMAT vs NACRE II), propagating rate uncertainties via Monte Carlo posterior sampling.
skills.name: deuterium-abundance-anomaly-comparison-across-rate-prescriptions
skills.search_text: deuterium-abundance-anomaly-comparison-across-rate-prescriptions Use when primordial deuterium (or lithium) abundance predictions from a BBN code must be compared under different nuclear-rate compilations (PRIMAT vs NACRE II), propagating rate uncertainties via Monte Carlo posterior sampling. When a single fixed-rate BBN point prediction suffices (no rate-uncertainty marginalization needed) — a direct PRyMordial run is cheaper than the full emcee double-run. When the question is Standard-Model thermal-background physics (N_eff, neutron-to-proton conversion) rather than nuclear-rate-systematics comparison. When only one rate compilation is of interest — the skill's value comes from the PRIMAT-vs-NACRE II contrast, not from either run alone. Runs PRyMordial's BBN Monte Carlo twice — once with PRIMAT thermonuclear rates and once with NACRE II rates (nacreii_flag on) — sampling 63 log-normal nuclear-rate nuisance parameters plus Gaussian-prior-constrained tau_n and Omega_B h^2, then compares marginalized posterior-predicted deuterium abundances against observation to test whether the deuterium anomaly persists or washes out under each rate prescription. astronomy/v1 10.1140/epjc/s10052-024-12442-0
skills.summary: Runs PRyMordial's BBN Monte Carlo twice — once with PRIMAT thermonuclear rates and once with NACRE II rates (nacreii_flag on) — sampling 63 log-normal nuclear-rate nuisance parameters plus Gaussian-prior-constrained tau_n and Omega_B h^2, then compares marginalized posterior-predicted deuterium abundances against observation to test whether the deuterium anomaly persists or washes out under each rate prescription.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a single fixed-rate BBN point prediction suffices (no rate-uncertainty marginalization needed) — a direct PRyMordial run is cheaper than the full emcee double-run. When the question is Standard-Model thermal-background physics (N_eff, neutron-to-proton conversion) rather than nuclear-rate-systematics comparison. When only one rate compilation is of interest — the skill's value comes from the PRIMAT-vs-NACRE II contrast, not from either run alone.

skills.summary: Derives rocky planet bulk compositions and devolatilisation patterns relative to host stars by extracting 50% condensation temperatures (Tc) of planet-building elements from equilibrium condensation simulations, then verifying abundance-pattern trends (Tc rising with metallicity, ~-100 K shift for C/O from 0.1 to 0.7) against real stellar data from the Brewer+2016 solar-neighbourhood sample.

skills.description: Use when sampling a Bayesian posterior over real-valued parameters (d ≈ 5–100+) where choosing jump scale/orientation for single-chain RWM is hard, or when benchmarking MCMC efficiency against WinBUGS or optimal-normal-jump random walk Metropolis.
skills.name: differential-evolution-markov-chain-sampling
skills.search_text: differential-evolution-markov-chain-sampling Use when sampling a Bayesian posterior over real-valued parameters (d ≈ 5–100+) where choosing jump scale/orientation for single-chain RWM is hard, or when benchmarking MCMC efficiency against WinBUGS or optimal-normal-jump random walk Metropolis. Discrete or non-real-parameter spaces — the difference-vector jump construction is defined over real parameter spaces only Posteriors with multiple distant modes when the initial population covers just a single modal region — far-away modes cannot be reached Problems needing a greedily fast sampler — DE-MC is explicitly not a greedy algorithm, a disadvantage in speed of convergence http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DE-MC) is a multi-chain MCMC method that proposes jumps as γ times the difference of two randomly chosen other chains, letting scale and orientation adapt automatically to the target's variance-covariance matrix for Bayesian computing in real parameter spaces. astronomy/v1 10.1007/s11222-006-8769-1
skills.summary: Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DE-MC) is a multi-chain MCMC method that proposes jumps as γ times the difference of two randomly chosen other chains, letting scale and orientation adapt automatically to the target's variance-covariance matrix for Bayesian computing in real parameter spaces.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Discrete or non-real-parameter spaces — the difference-vector jump construction is defined over real parameter spaces only Posteriors with multiple distant modes when the initial population covers just a single modal region — far-away modes cannot be reached Problems needing a greedily fast sampler — DE-MC is explicitly not a greedy algorithm, a disadvantage in speed of convergence

skills.description: Use when fitting Bayesian models on real parameter spaces where an appropriate scale and orientation for the jumping distribution is hard to choose, e.g. nonlinear mixed-effects models, and multi-chain MCMC should adapt jumps automatically via gamma = 2.38/sqrt(2d).
skills.name: differential-evolution-proposal-tuning
skills.search_text: differential-evolution-proposal-tuning Use when fitting Bayesian models on real parameter spaces where an appropriate scale and orientation for the jumping distribution is hard to choose, e.g. nonlinear mixed-effects models, and multi-chain MCMC should adapt jumps automatically via gamma = 2.38/sqrt(2d). The initial population covers only a single modal region — distant modes of a multimodal target cannot be reached, so DE-MC is the wrong choice for that exploration problem The target is restricted to generalized linear models where one-dimensional (e.g. Gibbs/WinBUGS) updates are natural and sufficient The problem requires a greedier, faster-converging sampler — plain DE-MC is deliberately not greedy, so convergence speed suffers http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Constructs the DE-MC proposal kernel x_p = x_i + gamma*(x_R1 - x_R2) + e from ter Braak (2006), so that jump scale and orientation are learned automatically from the population of chains instead of hand-tuned, with default gamma = 2.38/sqrt(2d) and a small symmetric perturbation e. astronomy/v1 10.1007/s11222-006-8769-1
skills.summary: Constructs the DE-MC proposal kernel x_p = x_i + gamma*(x_R1 - x_R2) + e from ter Braak (2006), so that jump scale and orientation are learned automatically from the population of chains instead of hand-tuned, with default gamma = 2.38/sqrt(2d) and a small symmetric perturbation e.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The initial population covers only a single modal region — distant modes of a multimodal target cannot be reached, so DE-MC is the wrong choice for that exploration problem The target is restricted to generalized linear models where one-dimensional (e.g. Gibbs/WinBUGS) updates are natural and sufficient The problem requires a greedier, faster-converging sampler — plain DE-MC is deliberately not greedy, so convergence speed suffers
