skills.name: hds-hdf5-file-format-conversion
skills.search_text: hds-hdf5-file-format-conversion Use when legacy HDS/HDSv4 astronomy data files (NDF images, ADAM parameter files, SCUBA-2 acquisition files) must be written or re-expressed as HDF5 via the HDSv5 drop-in library, or when comparing HDSv4 vs HDSv5 file sizes. skills.description: Use when comparing wall-clock performance of two drop-in file-format library builds — native HDSv4 versus the HDF5-backed hds-v5 — using the Starlink starbench, ccdpack, ccdbig and SCUBA-2 orac-dr benchmarks.
skills.name: hds-hdf5-library-benchmark-execution
skills.search_text: hds-hdf5-library-benchmark-execution Use when comparing wall-clock performance of two drop-in file-format library builds — native HDSv4 versus the HDF5-backed hds-v5 — using the Starlink starbench, ccdpack, ccdbig and SCUBA-2 orac-dr benchmarks. The goal is comparing output file sizes between HDSv4 and HDSv5 — that is the paper's separate size comparison, not benchmark timing execution. The library under test is not a drop-in replacement for the HDS API (locators, datMap/datUnmap, HDS groups); these benchmarks assume compatibility with the implemented HDS API functions. The systematic effect is gain variation or spin-synchronous contamination: destriping/binning alone can be ineffective or even harmful, and such effects must be handled before map-making. The scanning strategy lacks frequent crossing points between baselines, so baseline offsets cannot be constrained by pixel scatter. The goal is to remove high-frequency (white) noise rather than low-frequency correlated noise; binning/destriping acts as a high-pass filter and does not whiten pixel noise. http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Binning polarimeter timestreams (Q/U samples with pointing PHI/THETA) onto a HEALPix sky map, which serves both as the map-making baseline (plain binning) and as the binning operator B inside the destriping equation of the dst destriper. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.10.002

The disc requires radially dependent vertical structure or multiple disc planes — vis-r assumes a single disk plane with a fixed (radius-independent) vertical scale height The geometry is non-axisymmetric or needs a full 2D image-plane model; the DHT route only produces visibilities of a radial surface-brightness profile The input is not yet an averaged u,v dataset exported from an ms file — calibration/flagged data must first be discarded and averaged (e.g. 30 s intervals, a few channels per spw) http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Converts an arbitrary parametric radial surface-brightness profile I(r) directly into complex interferometric visibilities V(q) using the Discrete Hankel Transform, as implemented in vis-r as a matrix product, bypassing image-plane formation entirely. astronomy/v1 10.1093/rasti/rzaf004
skills.summary: Converts an arbitrary parametric radial surface-brightness profile I(r) directly into complex interferometric visibilities V(q) using the Discrete Hankel Transform, as implemented in vis-r as a matrix product, bypassing image-plane formation entirely.

skills.description: Use when a hyperspectral (IFU) unmixing problem needs a differentiable spectral model per physical component — e.g. APEC thermal plasma or synchrotron power-law spectra convolved with Chandra ARF/RMF responses — and the physical model itself is too slow or non-differentiable for optimization.
skills.name: interpolatory-autoencoder-decoding
skills.search_text: interpolatory-autoencoder-decoding Use when a hyperspectral (IFU) unmixing problem needs a differentiable spectral model per physical component — e.g. APEC thermal plasma or synchrotron power-law spectra convolved with Chandra ARF/RMF responses — and the physical model itself is too slow or non-differentiable for optimization. No spectral model (analytical or otherwise) is available for the physical components — SUSHI/IAE requires a fixed number of components each with a trainable spectral model A single call to the physical model is fast enough and gradients are available, so no learned surrogate is needed Target physical parameters fall outside the anchor-point parameter range, since the IAE only interpolates within the barycentric span of the anchor spectra http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains and applies an Interpolatory Auto-Encoder (IAE) — a generative, non-linear interpolatory model built from anchor-point spectra — as the learned spectral surrogate that SUSHI calls in place of slow physical models (e.g. APEC lookup tables via XSpec in Sherpa). The decoder D maps physical parameters (temperature, redshift, photon index) to spectra over 60x faster than the look-up-table-based physical model, enabling gradient-based unmixing. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202347518
skills.summary: Trains and applies an Interpolatory Auto-Encoder (IAE) — a generative, non-linear interpolatory model built from anchor-point spectra — as the learned spectral surrogate that SUSHI calls in place of slow physical models (e.g. APEC lookup tables via XSpec in Sherpa). The decoder D maps physical parameters (temperature, redshift, photon index) to spectra over 60x faster than the look-up-table-based physical model, enabling gradient-based unmixing.

skills.description: Use when you have vapour pressure (lnP, kPa) data for chemically heterogeneous compound classes (e.g. hydrocarbons plus organometallics like tetraorganostannanes) and need a single unified QSPR descriptor or a structural predictor of P.
skills.name: intrinsic-molar-volume-fragment-additivity
skills.search_text: intrinsic-molar-volume-fragment-additivity Use when you have vapour pressure (lnP, kPa) data for chemically heterogeneous compound classes (e.g. hydrocarbons plus organometallics like tetraorganostannanes) and need a single unified QSPR descriptor or a structural predictor of P. When the descriptor of interest is molecular weight: the article shows hydrocarbons and organostannanes (and organoplumbanes) form three parallel but distinct lnP–MW relationships, so any existing MW-based relationship for hydrocarbons cannot be used with tetraorganostannanes. When estimating vapour pressures of solid tetraorganostannanes (MP > 25°C) directly: Equation (9) values must first be converted to solid vapour pressures using entropy of fusion (ΔSf) and melting point. When the target compounds are tetraalkenylstannanes: current hydrocarbon-based estimation methods proved less successful for these, and the paper provides no validated alternative. Computes intrinsic molar volumes (V, cm3/mol) for compounds via the Hickey and Passino-Reader fragment additivity procedure and demonstrates that lnP of both hydrocarbons and tetraorganostannanes collapses onto a single linear QSPR in V, unlike molecular weight which yields parallel-but-distinct relationships. astronomy/v1 10.1016/0045-6535(92)90276-w
skills.summary: Computes intrinsic molar volumes (V, cm3/mol) for compounds via the Hickey and Passino-Reader fragment additivity procedure and demonstrates that lnP of both hydrocarbons and tetraorganostannanes collapses onto a single linear QSPR in V, unlike molecular weight which yields parallel-but-distinct relationships.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the descriptor of interest is molecular weight: the article shows hydrocarbons and organostannanes (and organoplumbanes) form three parallel but distinct lnP–MW relationships, so any existing MW-based relationship for hydrocarbons cannot be used with tetraorganostannanes. When estimating vapour pressures of solid tetraorganostannanes (MP > 25°C) directly: Equation (9) values must first be converted to solid vapour pressures using entropy of fusion (ΔSf) and melting point. When the target compounds are tetraalkenylstannanes: current hydrocarbon-based estimation methods proved less successful for these, and the paper provides no validated alternative.

skills.when_to_use_negative: When the compound set includes tetraalkenylstannanes only with no reference hydrocarbons — the paper shows hydrocarbon-derived estimation methods are 'less successful for tetraalkenylstannanes', so the single-relationship assumption may not hold When molecular weight is the intended descriptor — the paper explicitly states 'any existing relationship involving MW for hydrocarbons can not be used with tetraorganostannes' When predicting solid-state vapour pressures of tetraorganostannanes with MP > 25°C, which additionally require entropy of fusion (ΔSf) and melting point to convert Equation (9) data

skills.search_text: involutive-mcmc-transition-kernel-construction Use when the GP covariance function cannot be fixed a priori for a time series (e.g. stellar variability or exoplanet transit flux data) and the kernel structure itself must be inferred as a latent discrete variable via SMC with involutive MCMC transitions. The covariance function is already known or fixed a priori and only hyperparameters need tuning — gallifrey's structure learning targets inferring the covariance structure itself from the time series. The dataset is very large and runtime is critical — the paper explicitly flags scalability to larger datasets (e.g. for missions like PLATO) as future algorithmic work. The task is not time series modelling/forecasting (e.g. purely spatial or image data) — the method is focused on time series such as stellar variability and transit light curves. http://edamontology.org/topic_3360 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Constructs the SMC transition (rejuvenation) step of gallifrey's Bayesian GP kernel structure learning loop: an involutive Markov chain Monte Carlo kernel that jointly updates the discrete GP kernel structure and continuous hyperparameters within JAX. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202554518
skills.summary: Constructs the SMC transition (rejuvenation) step of gallifrey's Bayesian GP kernel structure learning loop: an involutive Markov chain Monte Carlo kernel that jointly updates the discrete GP kernel structure and continuous hyperparameters within JAX.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The covariance function is already known or fixed a priori and only hyperparameters need tuning — gallifrey's structure learning targets inferring the covariance structure itself from the time series. The dataset is very large and runtime is critical — the paper explicitly flags scalability to larger datasets (e.g. for missions like PLATO) as future algorithmic work. The task is not time series modelling/forecasting (e.g. purely spatial or image data) — the method is focused on time series such as stellar variability and transit light curves.

skills.search_text: irregular-time-series-interpolation Use when observations arrive at irregular timestamps (e.g. decaying-oscillator series sampled non-uniformly over [0,3]) and a continuous path must be constructed before solving a neural differential equation. Observations are already on a regular grid — direct tensor input to the model is simpler and interpolation adds no timing information. The downstream model expects logsignature features over windows (neural CDE preprocessing per the thesis) rather than a raw piecewise-linear path. Data must stay in raw units for interpretability — normalising each channel to zero mean/unit variance changes the value scale and must be inverted at decode time. skills.search_text: l1-norm-convergence-order-analysis Use when you have numerical solutions of a hyperbolic PDE at multiple resolutions plus an exact analytic reference, and need to measure whether L1 error decreases and what convergence order the scheme attains. You lack an exact analytic reference solution — L1 norms cannot be computed without one The discretisation is non-conservative (like Eq 10 for primitive variables); the analysis will merely confirm convergence to the wrong weak solution rather than certify the scheme Resolution pairs do not differ by a factor of 2, since the order estimator log(error_i/error_{i-1})/log(1/2) assumes halved grid spacing http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Quantifies numerical scheme convergence by computing the L1-norm error of simulation output against an exact reference solution at successive grid resolutions and deriving the convergence order as log(error_i/error_{i-1})/log(1/2). In this paper it validates the PVRS scheme (and diagnoses the non-convergent FDM-only primitive-variable scheme) on relativistic Sod shock tubes and a static Gaussian profile. astronomy/v1 10.1371/journal.pone.0195494
skills.summary: Quantifies numerical scheme convergence by computing the L1-norm error of simulation output against an exact reference solution at successive grid resolutions and deriving the convergence order as log(error_i/error_{i-1})/log(1/2). In this paper it validates the PVRS scheme (and diagnoses the non-convergent FDM-only primitive-variable scheme) on relativistic Sod shock tubes and a static Gaussian profile.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You lack an exact analytic reference solution — L1 norms cannot be computed without one The discretisation is non-conservative (like Eq 10 for primitive variables); the analysis will merely confirm convergence to the wrong weak solution rather than certify the scheme Resolution pairs do not differ by a factor of 2, since the order estimator log(error_i/error_{i-1})/log(1/2) assumes halved grid spacing

skills.description: Use when a rebuilt or extended surrogate (e.g., larger mass ratios, longer durations, higher harmonic modes) must be certified accurate and fast before release or reuse.
skills.name: l2-linf-waveform-accuracy-validation
skills.search_text: l2-linf-waveform-accuracy-validation Use when a rebuilt or extended surrogate (e.g., larger mass ratios, longer durations, higher harmonic modes) must be certified accurate and fast before release or reuse. The waveform model was not produced by the offline-online greedy-basis/empirical-interpolant/fit surrogate pipeline, so there is no compact surrogate prediction cost O(mL + m*c_fit) to compare No fiducial EOB-LAL (or equivalent) waveforms are available at validation points, so L2/Linf errors cannot be computed against a reference The goal is interpolating or fitting new waveform data rather than validating an existing surrogate's accuracy and evaluation speed http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 http://edamontology.org/topic_3452 Validates a rebuilt gravitational-wave surrogate model by computing L2 and Linf waveform errors at validation parameter points against fiducial EOB-LAL waveforms, and checking evaluation times and speedups against Table I values, accepting the surrogate only if the >3-orders-of-magnitude speedup is retained. astronomy/v1 10.1103/physrevx.4.031006
skills.summary: Validates a rebuilt gravitational-wave surrogate model by computing L2 and Linf waveform errors at validation parameter points against fiducial EOB-LAL waveforms, and checking evaluation times and speedups against Table I values, accepting the surrogate only if the >3-orders-of-magnitude speedup is retained.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The waveform model was not produced by the offline-online greedy-basis/empirical-interpolant/fit surrogate pipeline, so there is no compact surrogate prediction cost O(mL + m*c_fit) to compare No fiducial EOB-LAL (or equivalent) waveforms are available at validation points, so L2/Linf errors cannot be computed against a reference The goal is interpolating or fitting new waveform data rather than validating an existing surrogate's accuracy and evaluation speed

skills.description: Use when you have irregularly-sampled continuous-time series, need generative modelling of latent dynamics, and must extrapolate far beyond the training window (e.g. train on [0, 3], test on [0, 12]).
skills.name: latent-ode-variational-inference
skills.search_text: latent-ode-variational-inference Use when you have irregularly-sampled continuous-time series, need generative modelling of latent dynamics, and must extrapolate far beyond the training window (e.g. train on [0, 3], test on [0, 12]). The task requires controlled (input-driven) dynamics rather than autonomous latent evolution — a neural CDE with an interpolated control path, not a latent ODE, is the appropriate model Long-term time dependencies must be learned directly by a recurrent encoder: the thesis notes the -h(t) term in the continuous-time GRU causes exponential decay of the hidden state, explaining why GRUs/LSTMs struggle to learn long-term dependencies Only short-horizon interpolation within the training window is needed — the variational latent ODE machinery is aimed at generative extrapolation beyond the training interval http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Train a latent ODE VAE (GRU encoder, neural ODE latent dynamics solved with diffrax Tsit5, Gaussian decoder) on irregularly-sampled decaying-oscillator time series over [0, 3] by maximising the ELBO, so the trained model can be rolled forward to generate samples over a four-times-longer horizon [0, 12]. astronomy/v1 10.48550/arxiv.2202.02435
skills.summary: Train a latent ODE VAE (GRU encoder, neural ODE latent dynamics solved with diffrax Tsit5, Gaussian decoder) on irregularly-sampled decaying-oscillator time series over [0, 3] by maximising the ELBO, so the trained model can be rolled forward to generate samples over a four-times-longer horizon [0, 12].
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires controlled (input-driven) dynamics rather than autonomous latent evolution — a neural CDE with an interpolated control path, not a latent ODE, is the appropriate model Long-term time dependencies must be learned directly by a recurrent encoder: the thesis notes the -h(t) term in the continuous-time GRU causes exponential decay of the hidden state, explaining why GRUs/LSTMs struggle to learn long-term dependencies Only short-horizon interpolation within the training window is needed — the variational latent ODE machinery is aimed at generative extrapolation beyond the training interval

skills.description: Use when two bodies are on intersecting Kepler orbits and you need an analytic collision time from their orbital elements and period ratio, e.g. to jump directly between collision events instead of time-stepping.
skills.name: lattice-grid-point-closest-to-origin-geometry
skills.search_text: lattice-grid-point-closest-to-origin-geometry Use when two bodies are on intersecting Kepler orbits and you need an analytic collision time from their orbital elements and period ratio, e.g. to jump directly between collision events instead of time-stepping. Collision detection for bodies whose orbits are not well described by Keplerian two-body motion around a central mass (e.g. strong mutual interactions requiring full N-body integration). Systems where collisions are frequent and time-jumping offers no advantage — the article notes gravitational interactions can only be treated as scattering or secular perturbation, at the cost of reduced time-step or accuracy. http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Reduces the time-of-collision problem for two bodies on intersecting Kepler orbits to a lattice geometry problem: finding the grid point between two parallel lines closest to the origin, solved via the continued fraction of the orbital-period ratio. This yields an analytic, finite collision time enabling time-jumping propagation in N-body Keplerian systems. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202243754
skills.summary: Reduces the time-of-collision problem for two bodies on intersecting Kepler orbits to a lattice geometry problem: finding the grid point between two parallel lines closest to the origin, solved via the continued fraction of the orbital-period ratio. This yields an analytic, finite collision time enabling time-jumping propagation in N-body Keplerian systems.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Collision detection for bodies whose orbits are not well described by Keplerian two-body motion around a central mass (e.g. strong mutual interactions requiring full N-body integration). The goal is a full multidimensional parameter-space exploration (e.g. varying common-envelope physics and the LBV rate jointly) — the paper explicitly varies individual parameters independently and defers joint exploration to future studies. The study requires stellar rotation, tides, or wind accretion by companions — these physical processes are not included in the Fiducial model, so COMPAS results under this skill would not capture them. Reproduces the paper's low-metallicity (Z=0.001, 5% solar) BBH progenitor analysis in COMPAS: run the Fiducial population synthesis and single-parameter variants (e.g. LBV wind 1.5e-4 → 1e-3 Msun/yr) with STROOPWAFEL sampling, then compare total Hubble-time BBH merger yields and LVT151012-like (progenitor total mass ≳90 Msun) counts against Fiducial. astronomy/v1 10.1038/ncomms14906

skills.search_text: lte-spectroscopic-post-processing Use when you have an ExoMol, ExoMolHR, ExoAtom, HITRAN, or HITEMP molecular/atomic line list and need LTE or non-LTE stick spectra, cross-sections, or derived properties such as partition functions or cooling functions. skills.summary: Generate LTE (and non-LTE) absorption and emission stick spectra from huge molecular line lists using PyExoCross, a Python adaptation of the ExoCross Fortran code, with temperature-weighted line intensities computed via the partition function.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a smoothed/broadened spectrum rather than discrete line positions and intensities — use the cross-section computation with Doppler/Gaussian/Lorentzian/Voigt profiles instead of StickSpectra. skills.description: Use when sampling from a Bayesian posterior or other target density on a real parameter space of dimension d where choosing the scale and orientation of a jumping distribution is hard, and block/multi-chain updating is desired.
skills.name: markov-chain-monte-carlo-sampler-implementation
skills.search_text: markov-chain-monte-carlo-sampler-implementation Use when sampling from a Bayesian posterior or other target density on a real parameter space of dimension d where choosing the scale and orientation of a jumping distribution is hard, and block/multi-chain updating is desired. The initial population covers only a single modal region — distant modes cannot be reached, so DE-MC is wrong for far-away mode discovery in that setting Speed of convergence is critical and a greedy optimizer is acceptable — DE-MC is not a greedy algorithm, which the paper notes is a disadvantage Large populations are required — the paper notes large populations require more computer time to converge than small ones http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Implement the DE-MC sampler of ter Braak (2006): a multi-chain Metropolis MCMC whose jump is x_p = x_i + γ(x_R1 − x_R2) + e, where the difference of two randomly chosen other chains supplies scale and orientation adapted to the target's variance-covariance matrix. astronomy/v1 10.1007/s11222-006-8769-1
skills.summary: Implement the DE-MC sampler of ter Braak (2006): a multi-chain Metropolis MCMC whose jump is x_p = x_i + γ(x_R1 − x_R2) + e, where the difference of two randomly chosen other chains supplies scale and orientation adapted to the target's variance-covariance matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The initial population covers only a single modal region — distant modes cannot be reached, so DE-MC is wrong for far-away mode discovery in that setting Speed of convergence is critical and a greedy optimizer is acceptable — DE-MC is not a greedy algorithm, which the paper notes is a disadvantage Large populations are required — the paper notes large populations require more computer time to converge than small ones

skills.description: Use when you need to draw samples from a real-parameter-space target density (e.g. a high-dimensional posterior) and want an MCMC that avoids hand-tuning the jump distribution's scale and orientation.
skills.name: markov-chain-monte-carlo-target-density-specification
skills.search_text: markov-chain-monte-carlo-target-density-specification Use when you need to draw samples from a real-parameter-space target density (e.g. a high-dimensional posterior) and want an MCMC that avoids hand-tuning the jump distribution's scale and orientation. If the initial population covers just a single modal region, distant modes cannot be reached — do not expect DE-MC to discover far-away modes from a single-modal start. When you need one-dimensional block updates inside a generalized linear model context, WinBUGS-style samplers may suffice; DE-MC targets real parameter spaces where jump scale/orientation choice is the bottleneck. When a greedy optimizer is needed for speed: DE-MC is not a greedy algorithm, which is a disadvantage in terms of speed of convergence. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Specify a target log-density (e.g. a d=100 standard Normal) and sample it with Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DE-MC), in which N parallel chains initialized from overdispersed states learn from each other and self-tune jump scale and orientation to the target's variance-covariance matrix. astronomy/v1 10.1007/s11222-006-8769-1
skills.summary: Specify a target log-density (e.g. a d=100 standard Normal) and sample it with Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DE-MC), in which N parallel chains initialized from overdispersed states learn from each other and self-tune jump scale and orientation to the target's variance-covariance matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If the initial population covers just a single modal region, distant modes cannot be reached — do not expect DE-MC to discover far-away modes from a single-modal start. When you need one-dimensional block updates inside a generalized linear model context, WinBUGS-style samplers may suffice; DE-MC targets real parameter spaces where jump scale/orientation choice is the bottleneck. When a greedy optimizer is needed for speed: DE-MC is not a greedy algorithm, which is a disadvantage in terms of speed of convergence.

The goal is the average NFW concentration–mass relation or ΛCDM comparison rather than per-cluster residual structure Only parametric (NFW/Einasto) fits exist and no nonparametrically recovered profiles are available to compare against The mass profiles come from a model other than hydrostatic-equilibrium reconstruction of X-ray/SZ data (e.g. lensing-only profiles), where residual interpretation differs http://edamontology.org/topic_3360 Quantifies how well an NFW parametric model reproduces individually recovered hydrostatic mass profiles by computing fractional residuals (M_recovered - M_NFW)/M_NFW per radial bin, exposing per-cluster shape diversity beyond the NFW form. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202142507
skills.summary: Quantifies how well an NFW parametric model reproduces individually recovered hydrostatic mass profiles by computing fractional residuals (M_recovered - M_NFW)/M_NFW per radial bin, exposing per-cluster shape diversity beyond the NFW form.

skills.description: Use when reproducing or validating CONCEPT 1.0 Figure 2 time-step curves: you must identify which limiter (fixed-Δa, Hubble, dynamical, or non-linear P3M) governs Δln a at each scale factor and check the equality-transition feature.
skills.name: matter-lambda-equality-diagnostics
skills.search_text: matter-lambda-equality-diagnostics Use when reproducing or validating CONCEPT 1.0 Figure 2 time-step curves: you must identify which limiter (fixed-Δa, Hubble, dynamical, or non-linear P3M) governs Δln a at each scale factor and check the equality-transition feature. The goal is a power-spectrum code comparison (e.g. CONCEPT vs GADGET-2/GADGET-4 agreement at k ~ 13 h/Mpc) rather than time-step limiter behaviour. The analysis targets performance scaling (weak/strong scaling up to 1024 CPU cores) or code installation/build diagnostics rather than the time-stepping scheme. Fluid-component time-stepping is the target in releases prior to v0.2.0, which contained an erroneous time-stepping limiter for fluid components. http://edamontology.org/topic_3307 Diagnoses the matter–Λ equality transition in the CONCEPT 1.0 global time-step scheme by evaluating the fixed-Δa limiter branches (constant early and late branches transitioning around matter–Λ equality), combining all limiters pointwise with NumPy, and verifying the transition feature and resolution ordering in Figure 2-style Δln a(a) curves. astronomy/v1 10.1093/mnras/stac568
skills.summary: Diagnoses the matter–Λ equality transition in the CONCEPT 1.0 global time-step scheme by evaluating the fixed-Δa limiter branches (constant early and late branches transitioning around matter–Λ equality), combining all limiters pointwise with NumPy, and verifying the transition feature and resolution ordering in Figure 2-style Δln a(a) curves.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a power-spectrum code comparison (e.g. CONCEPT vs GADGET-2/GADGET-4 agreement at k ~ 13 h/Mpc) rather than time-step limiter behaviour. The analysis targets performance scaling (weak/strong scaling up to 1024 CPU cores) or code installation/build diagnostics rather than the time-stepping scheme. Fluid-component time-stepping is the target in releases prior to v0.2.0, which contained an erroneous time-stepping limiter for fluid components.

skills.description: Use when comparing sampler efficiency (e.g. emcee/CosmoHammer vs Metropolis-Hastings CosmoMC) by estimating autocorrelation times per parameter, or when determining the sampling effort needed to reach a target statistical error epsilon <= 0.1.
skills.name: mcmc-autocorrelation-time-analysis
skills.search_text: mcmc-autocorrelation-time-analysis Use when comparing sampler efficiency (e.g. emcee/CosmoHammer vs Metropolis-Hastings CosmoMC) by estimating autocorrelation times per parameter, or when determining the sampling effort needed to reach a target statistical error epsilon <= 0.1. Chains are not yet converged or burn-in b is unknown — epsilon computed from Eq. 8 with a wrong b is meaningless The sampler is not a Goodman-Weare ensemble sampler and the Appendix C estimator assumptions (exponential autocorrelation) do not apply The goal is wall-time scaling analysis (e.g. 30 h on dual core to 16 min on 2048 cores) rather than statistical error of the sample http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Estimate per-parameter autocorrelation times (tau) of MCMC chains using the Goodman-Weare Appendix C estimator (acor package), and use them to quantify the statistical error epsilon = |2*tau/((n-b)*L)|^(1/2) as a function of walkers L, sequential steps n, and burn-in b. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.06.003
skills.summary: Estimate per-parameter autocorrelation times (tau) of MCMC chains using the Goodman-Weare Appendix C estimator (acor package), and use them to quantify the statistical error epsilon = |2*tau/((n-b)*L)|^(1/2) as a function of walkers L, sequential steps n, and burn-in b.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Chains are not yet converged or burn-in b is unknown — epsilon computed from Eq. 8 with a wrong b is meaningless The sampler is not a Goodman-Weare ensemble sampler and the Appendix C estimator assumptions (exponential autocorrelation) do not apply The goal is wall-time scaling analysis (e.g. 30 h on dual core to 16 min on 2048 cores) rather than statistical error of the sample

skills.description: Use when a C++/CBL analysis needs posterior sampling of cosmological model parameters via MCMC, with a chi-squared likelihood plus Gaussian priors, and chain/posterior outputs must be validated.
skills.name: mcmc-chain-convergence-and-marginal-posterior-analysis
skills.search_text: mcmc-chain-convergence-and-marginal-posterior-analysis Use when a C++/CBL analysis needs posterior sampling of cosmological model parameters via MCMC, with a chi-squared likelihood plus Gaussian priors, and chain/posterior outputs must be validated. The analysis only needs catalogue handling or correlation-function measurements (2PCF/3PCF) rather than posterior sampling — use CBL clustering/statistics classes instead The likelihood function is not expressible as a chi-squared likelihood with Gaussian priors in the cosmobl::MCMC framework and requires a different sampler framework Only Python wrapper functions are required — the article notes only a subset of the CBL has a Python wrapper, so MCMC work may require C++ Runs and post-processes MCMC chains from the CBL statistical analysis toolkit: single-particle Metropolis-Hastings (Hastings 1970) and multi-particle stretch-move (Goodman & Weare 2010) sampling of a user-defined posterior, with burn-in removal and marginalised 1D posteriors written to mcmc_chains.dat. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2016.01.005
skills.summary: Runs and post-processes MCMC chains from the CBL statistical analysis toolkit: single-particle Metropolis-Hastings (Hastings 1970) and multi-particle stretch-move (Goodman & Weare 2010) sampling of a user-defined posterior, with burn-in removal and marginalised 1D posteriors written to mcmc_chains.dat.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis only needs catalogue handling or correlation-function measurements (2PCF/3PCF) rather than posterior sampling — use CBL clustering/statistics classes instead The likelihood function is not expressible as a chi-squared likelihood with Gaussian priors in the cosmobl::MCMC framework and requires a different sampler framework Only Python wrapper functions are required — the article notes only a subset of the CBL has a Python wrapper, so MCMC work may require C++

skills.description: Use when building an extensible MCMC framework that must combine independent theory-prediction (core) and likelihood modules via a shared context, or when refactoring a monolithic likelihood computation into plug-in modules.
skills.name: mcmc-context-data-exchange-design
skills.search_text: mcmc-context-data-exchange-design Use when building an extensible MCMC framework that must combine independent theory-prediction (core) and likelihood modules via a shared context, or when refactoring a monolithic likelihood computation into plug-in modules. The likelihood computation is a single self-contained function with no theory/likelihood split — a plain callable passed to the sampler is simpler than a chain of modules The sampler used is not emcee-based and already provides its own module/plugin interface (e.g. CosmoMC's own module system) You only need to run an existing CosmoHammer plugin unchanged — use the cosmoHammerPlugins modules directly rather than redesigning the chain http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 http://edamontology.org/topic_3452 Designs a modular MCMC likelihood pipeline (as in CosmoHammer's LikelihoodComputationChain) where self-contained core modules (e.g. CAMB theory predictions) and likelihood modules (e.g. WMAP) exchange data via a shared chain context (ctx) object, assembled in a defined order with parameter bounds enforced. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.06.003
skills.summary: Designs a modular MCMC likelihood pipeline (as in CosmoHammer's LikelihoodComputationChain) where self-contained core modules (e.g. CAMB theory predictions) and likelihood modules (e.g. WMAP) exchange data via a shared chain context (ctx) object, assembled in a defined order with parameter bounds enforced.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The likelihood computation is a single self-contained function with no theory/likelihood split — a plain callable passed to the sampler is simpler than a chain of modules The sampler used is not emcee-based and already provides its own module/plugin interface (e.g. CosmoMC's own module system) You only need to run an existing CosmoHammer plugin unchanged — use the cosmoHammerPlugins modules directly rather than redesigning the chain

skills.description: Use when a radial-velocity time series contains an unknown number of planetary signals and you need the sampler itself to decide how many Keplerian components to keep, with posteriors from each run seeding the next and a tolerance-based stopping rule.
skills.name: mcmc-convergence-and-posterior-constraining
skills.search_text: mcmc-convergence-and-posterior-constraining Use when a radial-velocity time series contains an unknown number of planetary signals and you need the sampler itself to decide how many Keplerian components to keep, with posteriors from each run seeding the next and a tolerance-based stopping rule. The number of planets or the model structure is already known and fixed — a single MCMC run without the autorun comparison loop suffices The input is not an RV (or RV+astrometry) time series; EMPEROR's Keplerian/Offset/Jitter blocks and comparison loop are built for orbital signal retrieval The result will be accepted on statistics alone — the paper notes purely statistical inference might be insufficient for robust exoplanet detection An automated iterative MCMC model-selection loop (EMPEROR) that samples each candidate Keplerian model with adaptive parallel tempering, applies convergence tests and Bayesian statistics, and constrains each new run's priors from the previous run's posteriors until the comparison statistic (BIC or Evidence) stops improving. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202554336
skills.summary: An automated iterative MCMC model-selection loop (EMPEROR) that samples each candidate Keplerian model with adaptive parallel tempering, applies convergence tests and Bayesian statistics, and constrains each new run's priors from the previous run's posteriors until the comparison statistic (BIC or Evidence) stops improving.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The number of planets or the model structure is already known and fixed — a single MCMC run without the autorun comparison loop suffices The input is not an RV (or RV+astrometry) time series; EMPEROR's Keplerian/Offset/Jitter blocks and comparison loop are built for orbital signal retrieval The result will be accepted on statistics alone — the paper notes purely statistical inference might be insufficient for robust exoplanet detection

skills.description: Use when comparing two sampler backends (e.g. emcee ensemble MCMC vs stan HMC/NUTS) on the same visibility likelihood, or when deciding whether a posterior run has converged before trusting parameter estimates.
skills.name: mcmc-convergence-diagnostic-analysis
skills.search_text: mcmc-convergence-diagnostic-analysis Use when comparing two sampler backends (e.g. emcee ensemble MCMC vs stan HMC/NUTS) on the same visibility likelihood, or when deciding whether a posterior run has converged before trusting parameter estimates. Input is a single already-converged posterior with no alternative sampler run to compare against and only qualitative trace inspection is needed The model uses the emcee-only --astrom independent astrometry fitting option, which has no stan counterpart and would make sampler comparison invalid Likelihood evaluation is so cheap that ESS efficiency gains do not matter (e.g. tiny u,v-averaged datasets where emcee already completes quickly) http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Compute convergence diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample size, trace stability) with arviz for MCMC posteriors fitted with vis-r, specifically to validate swapping the emcee sampler for the gradient-based stan HMC/NUTS implementation at equal warmup/sampling step budgets. astronomy/v1 10.1093/rasti/rzaf004
skills.summary: Compute convergence diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample size, trace stability) with arviz for MCMC posteriors fitted with vis-r, specifically to validate swapping the emcee sampler for the gradient-based stan HMC/NUTS implementation at equal warmup/sampling step budgets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single already-converged posterior with no alternative sampler run to compare against and only qualitative trace inspection is needed The model uses the emcee-only --astrom independent astrometry fitting option, which has no stan counterpart and would make sampler comparison invalid Likelihood evaluation is so cheap that ESS efficiency gains do not matter (e.g. tiny u,v-averaged datasets where emcee already completes quickly)

skills.description: Use when you have posterior chains from ensemble (Goodman-Weare/emcee) or Metropolis-Hastings MCMC samplers and need per-parameter autocorrelation times to compare sampler convergence and efficiency side by side.
skills.name: mcmc-convergence-diagnostic-tabulation
skills.search_text: mcmc-convergence-diagnostic-tabulation Use when you have posterior chains from ensemble (Goodman-Weare/emcee) or Metropolis-Hastings MCMC samplers and need per-parameter autocorrelation times to compare sampler convergence and efficiency side by side. Input is not MCMC chain time series data (e.g. you need raw likelihood values or best-fit points from particle swarm optimization rather than convergence diagnostics). Chains are too short or not yet mixed relative to the expected tau — the acor estimator requires sufficiently long, stationary series to yield reliable tau. The comparison target is wall-time scaling on distributed cores rather than per-parameter sampling efficiency. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Estimates and tabulates per-parameter autocorrelation times (tau) from MCMC chains using the Goodman-Weare exponential autocorrelation estimator (the acor package), enabling quantitative comparison of sampler efficiency, e.g. CosmoHammer/emcee versus fine-tuned and self-tuning CosmoMC Metropolis-Hastings runs on the WMAP 7 likelihood. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.06.003
skills.summary: Estimates and tabulates per-parameter autocorrelation times (tau) from MCMC chains using the Goodman-Weare exponential autocorrelation estimator (the acor package), enabling quantitative comparison of sampler efficiency, e.g. CosmoHammer/emcee versus fine-tuned and self-tuning CosmoMC Metropolis-Hastings runs on the WMAP 7 likelihood.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not MCMC chain time series data (e.g. you need raw likelihood values or best-fit points from particle swarm optimization rather than convergence diagnostics). Chains are too short or not yet mixed relative to the expected tau — the acor estimator requires sufficiently long, stationary series to yield reliable tau. The comparison target is wall-time scaling on distributed cores rather than per-parameter sampling efficiency.

skills.description: Use when an MCMC posterior sample of cosmological parameters (e.g. from CosmoHammer/emcee on WMAP 7 data) must be cross-checked against a reference sampler like CosmoMC to confirm convergence and statistical agreement within ~3.4%-of-sigma tolerance.
skills.name: mcmc-convergence-verification-against-reference
skills.search_text: mcmc-convergence-verification-against-reference Use when an MCMC posterior sample of cosmological parameters (e.g. from CosmoHammer/emcee on WMAP 7 data) must be cross-checked against a reference sampler like CosmoMC to confirm convergence and statistical agreement within ~3.4%-of-sigma tolerance. The WMAP likelihood data is not accessible on the filesystem and CFITSIO is not installed — the likelihood modules cannot be evaluated, so no posterior can be produced to verify. The goal is throughput/scalability benchmarking of the sampler rather than posterior correctness — use CosmoHammer's scaling analysis (2048-core timing) instead. The reference posterior comes from a different dataset (e.g. Planck) or a different parameter basis than the seven Λ-CDM parameters, making a 3.4%-of-sigma comparison meaningless. http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Verifies that a converged MCMC posterior (e.g. CosmoHammer/emcee on the seven Λ-CDM parameters against WMAP 7-year data) agrees with a reference chain such as CosmoMC within the expected statistical error of ~3.4% of the marginal standard deviation, at matched effective sample sizes. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.06.003
skills.summary: Verifies that a converged MCMC posterior (e.g. CosmoHammer/emcee on the seven Λ-CDM parameters against WMAP 7-year data) agrees with a reference chain such as CosmoMC within the expected statistical error of ~3.4% of the marginal standard deviation, at matched effective sample sizes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The WMAP likelihood data is not accessible on the filesystem and CFITSIO is not installed — the likelihood modules cannot be evaluated, so no posterior can be produced to verify. The goal is throughput/scalability benchmarking of the sampler rather than posterior correctness — use CosmoHammer's scaling analysis (2048-core timing) instead. The reference posterior comes from a different dataset (e.g. Planck) or a different parameter basis than the seven Λ-CDM parameters, making a 3.4%-of-sigma comparison meaningless.

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how many MCMC iterations are required before chains lose their initialisation bias, especially when comparing ensemble samplers with large walker counts L against Metropolis–Hastings chains.
skills.name: mcmc-ensemble-mean-tracking
skills.search_text: mcmc-ensemble-mean-tracking Use when you need to quantify how many MCMC iterations are required before chains lose their initialisation bias, especially when comparing ensemble samplers with large walker counts L against Metropolis–Hastings chains. When chains are Metropolis–Hastings without an accessible ensemble of independent walkers, the predicted error sigma/sqrt(L) must be reinterpreted per chain rather than per walker ensemble When samples are taken from the self-tuning CosmoMC proposal-tuning phase (~2000 steps), as those samples are not yet usable for inference When the goal is autocorrelation-time estimation itself rather than burn-in determination — use acor (dfm/acor) for tau estimation instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 http://edamontology.org/topic_3452 Determines MCMC burn-in length by monitoring the ensemble mean of sequential walker steps X̄_t against the predicted standard error of the mean sigma/sqrt(L), identifying when initialisation bias vanishes. Applied to CosmoHammer (emcee) and fine-tuned CosmoMC chains for six WMAP7 cosmological parameters. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.06.003
skills.summary: Determines MCMC burn-in length by monitoring the ensemble mean of sequential walker steps X̄_t against the predicted standard error of the mean sigma/sqrt(L), identifying when initialisation bias vanishes. Applied to CosmoHammer (emcee) and fine-tuned CosmoMC chains for six WMAP7 cosmological parameters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When chains are Metropolis–Hastings without an accessible ensemble of independent walkers, the predicted error sigma/sqrt(L) must be reinterpreted per chain rather than per walker ensemble When samples are taken from the self-tuning CosmoMC proposal-tuning phase (~2000 steps), as those samples are not yet usable for inference When the goal is autocorrelation-time estimation itself rather than burn-in determination — use acor (dfm/acor) for tau estimation instead

skills.description: Use when you need to estimate cosmological parameters (e.g. the seven Lambda-CDM parameters) from CMB data via MCMC, or benchmark a new sampler's posteriors against a CosmoMC reference chain.
skills.name: mcmc-ensemble-sampling-cosmological-parameters
skills.search_text: mcmc-ensemble-sampling-cosmological-parameters Use when you need to estimate cosmological parameters (e.g. the seven Lambda-CDM parameters) from CMB data via MCMC, or benchmark a new sampler's posteriors against a CosmoMC reference chain. The goal is a single best-fit point rather than a full posterior — the paper instead uses particle swarm optimization before MCMC for that purpose Only a small number of cores is available and wall time is dominated by per-step likelihood cost rather than parallelisable ensemble evaluation (Metropolis-Hastings with heavy overheads may not benefit) More MPI processes are launched than there are ensemble walkers — extra processes idle and scaling plateaus (observed at 64 nodes) http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Run parallelised affine-invariant ensemble MCMC (emcee via CosmoHammer) over Lambda-CDM parameters with CAMB and the WMAP 7-year likelihood to obtain converged posterior means and marginal standard deviations comparable to CosmoMC within a ~3.4%-of-sigma statistical error. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.06.003
skills.summary: Run parallelised affine-invariant ensemble MCMC (emcee via CosmoHammer) over Lambda-CDM parameters with CAMB and the WMAP 7-year likelihood to obtain converged posterior means and marginal standard deviations comparable to CosmoMC within a ~3.4%-of-sigma statistical error.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a single best-fit point rather than a full posterior — the paper instead uses particle swarm optimization before MCMC for that purpose Only a small number of cores is available and wall time is dominated by per-step likelihood cost rather than parallelisable ensemble evaluation (Metropolis-Hastings with heavy overheads may not benefit) More MPI processes are launched than there are ensemble walkers — extra processes idle and scaling plateaus (observed at 64 nodes)

skills.description: Use when fitting Kepler or ground-based transit light curves where classic chi-squared underestimates parameter uncertainties because the photometric noise contains a correlated (red) component.
skills.name: mcmc-gibbs-sampling
skills.search_text: mcmc-gibbs-sampling Use when fitting Kepler or ground-based transit light curves where classic chi-squared underestimates parameter uncertainties because the photometric noise contains a correlated (red) component. When the photometric noise is known to be purely uncorrelated (white) — the classic chi-squared likelihood suffices and the extra sigma_r parameter is unnecessary. When the input is already a set of published transit parameters or a derived table rather than a raw/normalized photometric time series that needs light-curve fitting. Runs TAP's Markov Chain Monte Carlo fitting of exoplanet transit light curves, in which a wavelet-based likelihood (Carter and Winn 2009) lets uncorrelated white noise (sigma_w) and 1/f correlated red noise (sigma_r) evolve as free parameters via Gibbs sampling instead of assuming noiseless correlations as in classic chi-squared. astronomy/v1 10.1155/2012/697967
skills.summary: Runs TAP's Markov Chain Monte Carlo fitting of exoplanet transit light curves, in which a wavelet-based likelihood (Carter and Winn 2009) lets uncorrelated white noise (sigma_w) and 1/f correlated red noise (sigma_r) evolve as free parameters via Gibbs sampling instead of assuming noiseless correlations as in classic chi-squared.

skills.search_text: metropolis-acceptance-criterion-verification Use when implementing or auditing an MCMC sampler with difference-vector proposals (DE-MC scheme DE1) and you must confirm the proposal kernel is symmetric so a plain Metropolis ratio pi(x_p)/pi(x_i) is valid. When the proposal kernel is not symmetric (e.g. asymmetric or independent proposals), where a full Hastings ratio q(x_i, x_p)/q(x_p, x_i) is required instead of the plain Metropolis ratio. When the initial population covers only a single modal region and distant modes must be reached — the sampler cannot jump to far-away modes, so verification of the acceptance criterion will not fix the coverage problem. When one-dimensional updates suffice inside a generalized linear model context, where WinBUGS-style samplers are already adequate. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Verifies that a Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DE-MC) proposal defines a valid Metropolis step: because x_p = x_i + gamma*(x_R1 - x_R2) + e with symmetric random perturbation e, each jump must be as likely as the reverse jump given the current state of the remaining chains, and acceptance must follow min(1, pi(x_p)/pi(x_i)). astronomy/v1 10.1007/s11222-006-8769-1
skills.summary: Verifies that a Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DE-MC) proposal defines a valid Metropolis step: because x_p = x_i + gamma*(x_R1 - x_R2) + e with symmetric random perturbation e, each jump must be as likely as the reverse jump given the current state of the remaining chains, and acceptance must follow min(1, pi(x_p)/pi(x_i)).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the proposal kernel is not symmetric (e.g. asymmetric or independent proposals), where a full Hastings ratio q(x_i, x_p)/q(x_p, x_i) is required instead of the plain Metropolis ratio. When the initial population covers only a single modal region and distant modes must be reached — the sampler cannot jump to far-away modes, so verification of the acceptance criterion will not fix the coverage problem. When one-dimensional updates suffice inside a generalized linear model context, where WinBUGS-style samplers are already adequate.

The analysis target is not CMB power-spectrum data (TT, TE, EE, BB, phi-phi, kappa-kappa) — candl is scoped to CMB band power measurements You need MCMC posterior sampling rather than Fisher forecasts — use the gradient-based sampler interfaces (Cobaya/MontePython/BlackJAX) instead of direct Fisher construction The likelihood must reproduce Planck clik files with legacy semantics — use clipy (the pure-Python clik replacement) rather than reinitialising from a candl .yaml Initialise a candl likelihood (candl.Like) directly from a mock CMB power-spectrum data set's .yaml file, bin the model spectra with window functions, and use the JAX-differentiable likelihood as the basis for exact Fisher forecasts (e.g. band power bin width optimisation) on that mock data set. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202449432
skills.summary: Initialise a candl likelihood (candl.Like) directly from a mock CMB power-spectrum data set's .yaml file, bin the model spectra with window functions, and use the JAX-differentiable likelihood as the basis for exact Fisher forecasts (e.g. band power bin width optimisation) on that mock data set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis target is not CMB power-spectrum data (TT, TE, EE, BB, phi-phi, kappa-kappa) — candl is scoped to CMB band power measurements You need MCMC posterior sampling rather than Fisher forecasts — use the gradient-based sampler interfaces (Cobaya/MontePython/BlackJAX) instead of direct Fisher construction The likelihood must reproduce Planck clik files with legacy semantics — use clipy (the pure-Python clik replacement) rather than reinitialising from a candl .yaml

skills.description: Use when you have an intrinsic 1D rotation curve (disk+bulge+halo mass model) and need beam-smeared mock-observed rotation/dispersion curves for a given sky-orientation and PSF, e.g. for benchmarking or forward-model fitting.
skills.name: mock-observation-simulation-of-galaxy-kinematics
skills.search_text: mock-observation-simulation-of-galaxy-kinematics Use when you have an intrinsic 1D rotation curve (disk+bulge+halo mass model) and need beam-smeared mock-observed rotation/dispersion curves for a given sky-orientation and PSF, e.g. for benchmarking or forward-model fitting. The galaxy is not rotationally supported (V/sigma_0 <~ 2) or lacks a well-defined kinematic axis / has strong deviations from circular motions — the axisymmetric forward model assumes none The system is poorly resolved (beam size much larger than R_eff): the fitting procedure performs best for PSF <~ R_eff, and mock-observed curves can deviate up to ~15% even in marginally resolved cases Inclination is outside 10° < i < 80°, where RotCurves is best suited http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 Simulates the instrumental observation of an idealized axisymmetric galaxy model by projecting and convolving the beam PSF in the plane of the galaxy, reconstructing beam-smeared rotation and dispersion curves from the intrinsic equilibrium rotation velocity. astronomy/v1 10.1093/mnras/stag134
skills.summary: Simulates the instrumental observation of an idealized axisymmetric galaxy model by projecting and convolving the beam PSF in the plane of the galaxy, reconstructing beam-smeared rotation and dispersion curves from the intrinsic equilibrium rotation velocity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The galaxy is not rotationally supported (V/sigma_0 <~ 2) or lacks a well-defined kinematic axis / has strong deviations from circular motions — the axisymmetric forward model assumes none The system is poorly resolved (beam size much larger than R_eff): the fitting procedure performs best for PSF <~ R_eff, and mock-observed curves can deviate up to ~15% even in marginally resolved cases Inclination is outside 10° < i < 80°, where RotCurves is best suited

skills.description: Use when comparing population-level model predictions of 12CO fluxes against observed ALMA fluxes (e.g. Lupus or Upper Sco samples) and you need to quantify model-data agreement and its sensitivity to initial-condition uncertainties.
skills.name: model-data-agreement-quantification
skills.search_text: model-data-agreement-quantification Use when comparing population-level model predictions of 12CO fluxes against observed ALMA fluxes (e.g. Lupus or Upper Sco samples) and you need to quantify model-data agreement and its sensitivity to initial-condition uncertainties. When computationally-expensive thermochemical models (e.g. DALI) are needed for detailed physico-chemical modelling of individual discs — the semi-analytical approach trades chemical detail for speed (agreement only within a factor of three). When the sample has disc sizes but no measured 12CO fluxes and flux-based sample growth (1.3x Lupus, 3.6x Upper Sco) is not achievable from the available data. Quantifies how well semi-analytical 12CO flux predictions agree with observed ALMA fluxes of disc populations (Lupus, Upper Sco), including how the agreement spreads when model initial conditions (disc mass, radius) are varied. It provides the benchmarked factor-of-three accuracy framing used to judge whether a fast CO-flux model is trustworthy against both DALI thermochemical models and real data. astronomy/v1 10.1051/0004-6361/202346164
skills.summary: Quantifies how well semi-analytical 12CO flux predictions agree with observed ALMA fluxes of disc populations (Lupus, Upper Sco), including how the agreement spreads when model initial conditions (disc mass, radius) are varied. It provides the benchmarked factor-of-three accuracy framing used to judge whether a fast CO-flux model is trustworthy against both DALI thermochemical models and real data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When computationally-expensive thermochemical models (e.g. DALI) are needed for detailed physico-chemical modelling of individual discs — the semi-analytical approach trades chemical detail for speed (agreement only within a factor of three). When the sample has disc sizes but no measured 12CO fluxes and flux-based sample growth (1.3x Lupus, 3.6x Upper Sco) is not achievable from the available data.

skills.search_text: monte-carlo-rejection-filtering Use when simulating X-ray polarimetric observations where an instrumental effect (vignetting vs. off-axis angle, chip fiducial area, readout dead-time) must be realized by stochastic event rejection rather than deterministic reweighting. Analyzing real, already-corrected IXPE level-2 event lists where vignetting and dead-time corrections are applied analytically rather than by Monte Carlo rejection Bin-level analysis (e.g. PHA1/PCUBE products via xpbin) — rejection filtering operates on unbinned event lists during simulation, not on binned data products Detectors whose instrumental effects (e.g. non-paralyzable dead-time, chip gap geometry) are not representable as independent per-event rejection probabilities Monte Carlo rejection sampling as used in ixpeobssim to realize instrumental effects: one-dimensional pdfs are sampled via interpolated splines built from the cumulative function (ppf), and corrections such as vignetting, fiducial-area clipping, and dead-time are applied by randomly discarding events with the proper statistical dependence. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.softx.2022.101194
skills.summary: Monte Carlo rejection sampling as used in ixpeobssim to realize instrumental effects: one-dimensional pdfs are sampled via interpolated splines built from the cumulative function (ppf), and corrections such as vignetting, fiducial-area clipping, and dead-time are applied by randomly discarding events with the proper statistical dependence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Analyzing real, already-corrected IXPE level-2 event lists where vignetting and dead-time corrections are applied analytically rather than by Monte Carlo rejection Bin-level analysis (e.g. PHA1/PCUBE products via xpbin) — rejection filtering operates on unbinned event lists during simulation, not on binned data products Detectors whose instrumental effects (e.g. non-paralyzable dead-time, chip gap geometry) are not representable as independent per-event rejection probabilities

skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is wall-time/parallel-scaling benchmarking of the sampler rather than convergence/burn-in determination The chains come from a single-walker sampler where the ensemble mean vs sigma/sqrt(L) criterion does not apply Samples are needed only after the CosmoMC proposal-tuning phase (~2000 steps) has already been run — then the tuning phase, not the burn-in analysis, is the limiting step

skills.name: mpi-openmp-hybrid-parallelism-interpretation
skills.search_text: mpi-openmp-hybrid-parallelism-interpretation Use when interpreting or transcribing strong-scaling performance results (core counts, threading mixes, compilers) for hybrid MPI/OpenMP runs of AMReX-based codes like Castro on leadership-class machines such as OLCF Titan. The input is raw timing data from runs you executed yourself rather than reported scaling behavior to transcribe from a publication The scaling study concerns GPU-accelerated execution (CUDA/HIP/SYCL) rather than the MPI/OpenMP hybrid CPU parallelism reported here The question is about algorithmic capabilities of the codes (e.g., subsonic vs. compressible flow modeling) rather than parallel performance http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 Interprets published strong-scaling results for MPI/OpenMP hybrid execution of AMReX-based codes (Castro), extracting scaling behavior, maximum core counts, threading mixes, and compiler stacks into a structured record. It captures the reported finding that fewer MPI ranks with more OpenMP threads per rank performs best for multilevel AMR problems. astronomy/v1 10.1088/1742-6596/1031/1/012024
skills.summary: Interprets published strong-scaling results for MPI/OpenMP hybrid execution of AMReX-based codes (Castro), extracting scaling behavior, maximum core counts, threading mixes, and compiler stacks into a structured record. It captures the reported finding that fewer MPI ranks with more OpenMP threads per rank performs best for multilevel AMR problems.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw timing data from runs you executed yourself rather than reported scaling behavior to transcribe from a publication The scaling study concerns GPU-accelerated execution (CUDA/HIP/SYCL) rather than the MPI/OpenMP hybrid CPU parallelism reported here The question is about algorithmic capabilities of the codes (e.g., subsonic vs. compressible flow modeling) rather than parallel performance

skills.description: Use when CMB polarimeter timestreams (e.g. HDF5 files with TIME, PHI, THETA, PSI, FLAG, TEMP, Q, U columns) need correlated-noise removal and the destriping equation's left-side matrix is too large to invert directly for modest-to-large datasets.
skills.name: mpi-parallel-destriping-execution
skills.search_text: mpi-parallel-destriping-execution Use when CMB polarimeter timestreams (e.g. HDF5 files with TIME, PHI, THETA, PSI, FLAG, TEMP, Q, U columns) need correlated-noise removal and the destriping equation's left-side matrix is too large to invert directly for modest-to-large datasets. Data contain systematic effects such as thermally induced gain variations (e.g. near sunrise/sunset) or spin-synchronous effects — destriping can be ineffective or even harmful and these must be masked or handled separately before map-making The scanning strategy lacks frequent crossing points, so the destriping equation is poorly constrained The noise is white or the 1/f knee frequency is above the scan rate with no removable low-frequency correlated component http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Runs the dst Python parallel destriper under MPI (mpirun) on HDF5 polarimeter timelines to remove low-frequency correlated noise via iterative GMRES/CG baseline estimation, avoiding explicit inversion of the heavy left-side destriping matrix. astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.10.002
skills.summary: Runs the dst Python parallel destriper under MPI (mpirun) on HDF5 polarimeter timelines to remove low-frequency correlated noise via iterative GMRES/CG baseline estimation, avoiding explicit inversion of the heavy left-side destriping matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data contain systematic effects such as thermally induced gain variations (e.g. near sunrise/sunset) or spin-synchronous effects — destriping can be ineffective or even harmful and these must be masked or handled separately before map-making The scanning strategy lacks frequent crossing points, so the destriping equation is poorly constrained The noise is white or the 1/f knee frequency is above the scan rate with no removable low-frequency correlated component

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how wall time of an MCMC likelihood chain (e.g. CAMB + WMAP likelihood) scales with core count on a cluster, cloud (EC2), or grid, and to measure parallelisation overhead.
skills.name: mpi-parallel-mcmc-scaling-benchmarking
skills.search_text: mpi-parallel-mcmc-scaling-benchmarking Use when you need to quantify how wall time of an MCMC likelihood chain (e.g. CAMB + WMAP likelihood) scales with core count on a cluster, cloud (EC2), or grid, and to measure parallelisation overhead. The number of MPI processes exceeds the number of ensemble walkers (e.g. >300 walkers for a ratio of 50 with 6 parameters) — extra processes idle and the scaling curve plateaus rather than informs The goal is posterior inference or likelihood values themselves — this skill benchmarks wall-time scaling and reports no numeric likelihoods or posterior results Serial or embarrassingly parallel workloads without an ensemble MCMC structure — Metropolis–Hastings is dominated by overheads and will not exhibit the same scalability http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 http://edamontology.org/topic_3360 Benchmark the wall-time scaling of MPI-parallelised MCMC ensemble sampling (CosmoHammer/embedding emcee) across increasing core counts and fit a log-log power law to obtain the scaling exponent alpha (e.g. alpha = 0.89, an 11% overhead per doubling of cores). astronomy/v1 10.1016/j.ascom.2013.06.003
skills.summary: Benchmark the wall-time scaling of MPI-parallelised MCMC ensemble sampling (CosmoHammer/embedding emcee) across increasing core counts and fit a log-log power law to obtain the scaling exponent alpha (e.g. alpha = 0.89, an 11% overhead per doubling of cores).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The number of MPI processes exceeds the number of ensemble walkers (e.g. >300 walkers for a ratio of 50 with 6 parameters) — extra processes idle and the scaling curve plateaus rather than informs The goal is posterior inference or likelihood values themselves — this skill benchmarks wall-time scaling and reports no numeric likelihoods or posterior results Serial or embarrassingly parallel workloads without an ensemble MCMC structure — Metropolis–Hastings is dominated by overheads and will not exhibit the same scalability

skills.description: Use when you must quantify how an MPI-parallel PDE solver scales to large core counts — i.e., you have per-run timings for fixed-size (strong) or fixed-per-rank (weak) 3D spectral problems and need parallel-efficiency curves.
skills.name: mpi-parallel-strong-scaling-analysis
skills.search_text: mpi-parallel-strong-scaling-analysis Use when you must quantify how an MPI-parallel PDE solver scales to large core counts — i.e., you have per-run timings for fixed-size (strong) or fixed-per-rank (weak) 3D spectral problems and need parallel-efficiency curves. The workload is a serial or OpenMP-only code with no MPI domain decomposition (pencil/transform layout), so no per-core-count MPI timings exist The goal is correctness verification rather than performance — the Dedalus test suite (`python3 -m dedalus test`) and eigenvalue comparisons (e.g., waves-on-a-string relative error) are the right tool The problem is small enough to fit comfortably on one node, so parallel efficiency below the ~8-pencils-per-core regime is uninformative http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 Benchmarks MPI-parallel scientific codes (e.g., Dedalus's 3D Boussinesq hydro/MHD IVP benchmarks) by measuring wall-clock times across core counts, computing strong-scaling parallel efficiency and weak-scaling cost normalized per core, and validating the expected 1/log2(N) weak-scaling trend of FFT-based spectral methods. astronomy/v1 10.1103/physrevresearch.2.023068
skills.summary: Benchmarks MPI-parallel scientific codes (e.g., Dedalus's 3D Boussinesq hydro/MHD IVP benchmarks) by measuring wall-clock times across core counts, computing strong-scaling parallel efficiency and weak-scaling cost normalized per core, and validating the expected 1/log2(N) weak-scaling trend of FFT-based spectral methods.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The workload is a serial or OpenMP-only code with no MPI domain decomposition (pencil/transform layout), so no per-core-count MPI timings exist The goal is correctness verification rather than performance — the Dedalus test suite (`python3 -m dedalus test`) and eigenvalue comparisons (e.g., waves-on-a-string relative error) are the right tool The problem is small enough to fit comfortably on one node, so parallel efficiency below the ~8-pencils-per-core regime is uninformative

skills.description: Use when a PDE simulation must be time-integrated to a statistically saturated state (e.g., t=200) over a multi-dimensional spectral domain (e.g., 256x128x32 modes) and serial runtime is infeasible, requiring MPI parallelism.
skills.name: mpi-parallel-time-integration
skills.search_text: mpi-parallel-time-integration Use when a PDE simulation must be time-integrated to a statistically saturated state (e.g., t=200) over a multi-dimensional spectral domain (e.g., 256x128x32 modes) and serial runtime is infeasible, requiring MPI parallelism. The problem fits in a small dense/sparse eigenvalue solve (e.g., Mathieu eigenvalues, Rayleigh-Benard growth rates via solve_sparse) where simple dedicated solvers suffice without long time integration A quick serial integration to early times is adequate; MPI setup overhead (parallel HDF5, MPI-FFTW builds) is not justified The target system lacks an MPI toolchain (mpiicc/mpiicpc/mpiifort) needed to build parallel HDF5 and FFTW support Run long Dedalus spectral simulations (e.g., the 3D quasigeostrophic baroclinic instability example integrated to t=200) as MPI-parallel time integrations using Dedalus's compiled sparse solvers, producing HDF5 snapshot output of fields like potential vorticity (p) and buoyancy (w). astronomy/v1 10.1103/physrevresearch.2.023068
skills.summary: Run long Dedalus spectral simulations (e.g., the 3D quasigeostrophic baroclinic instability example integrated to t=200) as MPI-parallel time integrations using Dedalus's compiled sparse solvers, producing HDF5 snapshot output of fields like potential vorticity (p) and buoyancy (w).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The problem fits in a small dense/sparse eigenvalue solve (e.g., Mathieu eigenvalues, Rayleigh-Benard growth rates via solve_sparse) where simple dedicated solvers suffice without long time integration A quick serial integration to early times is adequate; MPI setup overhead (parallel HDF5, MPI-FFTW builds) is not justified The target system lacks an MPI toolchain (mpiicc/mpiicpc/mpiifort) needed to build parallel HDF5 and FFTW support

skills.description: Use when strong-scaling timing data shows an upturn or discontinuity near the maximum processor count, and the run mixes hybrid MPI/OpenMP configurations across NUMA nodes — as in the Maestro 3-d XRB runs on Titan and Edison.
skills.name: mpi-thread-configuration-interpretation
skills.search_text: mpi-thread-configuration-interpretation Use when strong-scaling timing data shows an upturn or discontinuity near the maximum processor count, and the run mixes hybrid MPI/OpenMP configurations across NUMA nodes — as in the Maestro 3-d XRB runs on Titan and Edison. The scaling study is weak-scaling or a problem size other than the 3-d XRB strong-scaling setup reported in Figure 2 — the upturn interpretation is specific to that configuration switch. The runs use a single, fixed MPI/OpenMP configuration, so there is no thread-configuration change to attribute an upturn to. The target code is Castro (highly compressible explosion flows) rather than Maestro (subsonic convective flows); no such scaling interpretation is reported for Castro in this context. Interprets strong-scaling curves for the Maestro 3-d X-ray burst (XRB) problem on OLCF Titan and NERSC Edison, attributing the end-of-curve performance upturn on Titan to a switch in MPI/OpenMP configuration (1 MPI task / 8 OpenMP threads per NUMA node to 1 MPI task / 16 threads) rather than algorithmic improvement. astronomy/v1 10.1088/1742-6596/1031/1/012024
skills.summary: Interprets strong-scaling curves for the Maestro 3-d X-ray burst (XRB) problem on OLCF Titan and NERSC Edison, attributing the end-of-curve performance upturn on Titan to a switch in MPI/OpenMP configuration (1 MPI task / 8 OpenMP threads per NUMA node to 1 MPI task / 16 threads) rather than algorithmic improvement.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The scaling study is weak-scaling or a problem size other than the 3-d XRB strong-scaling setup reported in Figure 2 — the upturn interpretation is specific to that configuration switch. skills.name: mukhanov-sasaki-mode-integration
skills.search_text: mukhanov-sasaki-mode-integration Use when computing the scalar primordial power spectrum from an inflationary background: you need to integrate oscillatory cosmological perturbation modes over a k range after solving the background and locating the end of inflation. skills.when_to_use_negative: The ODE system is non-oscillatory or its frequency varies rapidly everywhere — the WKB approximation in pyoscode is only valid when the frequency changes slowly relative to the integration timescale The problem is the Airy or burst-equation demonstration cases (pyoscode.solve / C++ burst example) rather than the cosmological perturbation pipeline with Bunch-Davies initial conditions The frequency and friction terms are known constant arrays amenable to standard stiff/adaptive solvers without oscillatory stepping
